2-2/n. The infinite-class cost lower bound gives the other inequality. QED.

### What (4.1) does and does not compare

It compares *suprema over actions*. It does not assert that every action of a
given Burnside group has cost c_n. In particular it does not permit replacing
C^*(H) by the infimum cost C_*(H).

[DS] proves the already known-to-this-continuation statement C_*(B(m,n))=1 for
large odd n, and explicitly distinguishes it from fixed price one. The uniform
upper bound here leaves a nonzero interval between 1 and 2-2/n.

## 5. Two completely specified free actions, with conditional separation

Set Gamma=B(2,n)=<a,b>. Let

    pi:Gamma -> Z/nZ,       pi(a)=1, pi(b)=0,
    K=ker(pi),             [Gamma:K]=n.

Let alpha be the Bernoulli shift on Omega=[0,1]^Gamma with product Lebesgue
measure. Define another Gamma-action on Omega x Z/nZ with uniform measure on the
second factor by

    beta(g)(omega,j) = (g omega, j+pi(g)).                    (5.1)

Both actions are essentially free: freeness follows from their Bernoulli
coordinate. They are also ergodic. Alpha is Bernoulli ergodic; for beta, its
restriction to K on any one sheet is a Bernoulli K-action, hence ergodic, and
Gamma permutes the n sheets transitively.

### Theorem 5.1

For these two particular actions,

    Cost(alpha)=c_n,
    Cost(beta)=1+(c_n-1)/n.                                 (5.2)

Hence

    Cost(alpha)-Cost(beta)=(1-1/n)(c_n-1),                  (5.3)

and, unconditionally,

    1 <= Cost(beta) <= 1+1/n-2/n^2.                         (5.4)

### Proof

Gamma is finitely generated, so the Bernoulli maximality theorem gives
Cost(alpha)=C^*(Gamma)=c_n.

K has finite index, hence is finitely generated; it is infinite. Theorem 4.1
gives C^*(K)=c_n. Restriction of alpha to K is a Bernoulli K-action: the Gamma
coordinates split into n regular K-orbits, which can be regrouped as a product
base for a K-indexed Bernoulli shift. Thus Cost(alpha restricted to K)=c_n.

The subset Y=Omega x {0} is a complete section of beta's orbit relation and has
measure 1/n. Its restricted orbit relation is exactly that of alpha restricted
to K: a group element returns the second coordinate to zero precisely when it
belongs to K. Equation (1.1) therefore gives

    Cost(beta)-1=(1/n)(c_n-1).

The other formulas follow algebraically. QED.

This is an exact action-cost calculation *in terms of an undetermined number*.
It is not a verified pair of different costs until c_n>1 is established.

### The remaining dichotomy

If c_n=1, then every infinite subgroup covered by Theorem 4.1 has fixed price one.
If c_n>1, the two actions in (5.1) and (5.2) refute the universal Fixed Price
assertion, even with free ergodic actions.

Neither inequality c_n>1 nor equality c_n=1 has been proved here.

## 6. A tempting false inference, and the correct normalization

One might try to combine C^*(K)=C^*(Gamma)=c_n with the formula

    C^*(K)-1 = [Gamma:K]*(C^*(Gamma)-1)                      (UNPROVED HERE)

to obtain c_n=1. That would insert an additional unproved input. The known
finite-index formula for the *infimum over actions* does not authorize the same
formula for a specified restricted action or for upper cost. [AN, Section 5]
carefully distinguishes these questions.

The formula used in Section 5 is instead the established complete-section
induction formula. The sheet Omega x {0} is an actual measurable section of the
*new* action beta. The original Bernoulli Gamma-action alpha was not compressed
by merely restricting the acting group to K. These are different operations.

A useful normalization check: a finite relation with classes of size h has cost
1-1/h. Amplifying each class into d sheets gives cost 1-1/(dh), which equals
1+((1-1/h)-1)/d. This confirms the factor 1/d in the induced-action formula.

The second action beta must not be identified with a Bernoulli action merely
because it has a Bernoulli coordinate. It is not mixing: its sheet Y has measure
1/n, and for every g in the infinite subgroup K one has gY=Y, so
mu(Y intersection gY)=1/n rather than 1/n^2. Bernoulli actions are mixing, as
can be checked first on cylinder events by disjointness of distant finite
coordinate sets and then by approximation. This distinction alone does not
prove a difference of costs.

## 7. Why this does not close Benjamini–Schramm

The prior necessary exponential-pivotal condition remains conditional. This
continuation provides no upper bound uniform in radius on those conditional
pivotal counts.

There is still the established implication [L]

    no nonuniqueness interval on a Cayley graph -> fixed price one.

If c_n>1, that implication gives nonuniqueness for Cayley graphs of the relevant
finitely generated Burnside subgroups, while the actions above would refute
Fixed Price. If c_n=1, it supplies no percolation conclusion for these groups.
Neither side of this dichotomy settles the universal Benjamini–Schramm claim.

## 8. Finite verification and Cairn semantics

`scripts/replay_torsion.py` uses exact permutations in A5 and exact rational
probabilities. It checks centralizer intersections, the alternating detour path,
all selector configurations for a finite three-detour fixture, the independent
failure product, and induced-cost normalization. A5 is just a finite algebra
test fixture. Its finite cosets cannot verify the infinite hypothesis of
Proposition 2.1.

The script does not prove weak containment, Burnside algebra, infinite measured
connectivity, cost infima, or c_n=1/c_n>1. Those mathematical issues are addressed
only by the written arguments and published inputs stated above, with the last
dichotomy explicitly unresolved.

The additive Cairn package retains prior work as provenance. A dependency check
validates node syntax, references, and the recorded implication graph, not the
truth of a proof. Both universal goals remain OPEN. There is no route from the
new conditional counterexample formula to a solved universal goal without a
proved strict lower bound c_n>1.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

---

## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

---

bash -lc cat > /mnt/data/torsion-local-work/replay_local_sparsifiers.py <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Finite checks for the local torsion sparsifier proof.

No infinite Burnside group, invariant measure theorem, or conjecture is
verified here. The Heisenberg group is a finite test fixture, not an example
of the infinite hypotheses.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse
import itertools
import json
from collections import deque
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path


def mul(g: tuple[int, int, int], h: tuple[int, int, int], p: int = 3):
    x, y, z = g
    u, v, w = h
    return ((x + u) % p, (y + v) % p, (z + w + x * v) % p)


def power(g, k: int, p: int = 3):
    h = (0, 0, 0)
    for _ in range(k):
        h = mul(h, g, p)
    return h


def edge(x, y):
    return tuple(sorted((x, y)))


def cycle_checks():
    cases = 0
    for n in (3, 5, 7, 9, 11):
        for mask in range(1 << n):
            boundary = [bool((mask >> i & 1) != (mask >> ((i + 1) % n) & 1)) for i in range(n)]
            old = sum(boundary)
            for deleted in range(n):
                new = old - boundary[deleted]
                assert 2 * new >= old
                cases += 1
    return {"cycle_lengths": [3, 5, 7, 9, 11], "cut_deletion_pairs": cases}


def density_checks():
    cases = 0
    probabilities = []
    for lengths in ((2,), (2, 2), (2, 2, 2), (2, 2, 2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 3, 4)):
        coords = 1 + sum(lengths)
        intervals = []
        start = 1
        for size in lengths:
            intervals.append(range(start, start + size))
            start += size
        for q in (Fraction(1, 5), Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(1, 2)):
            total = Fraction(0)
            for mask in range(1 << coords):
                selected = bool(mask & 1)
                success = any(all(mask >> j & 1 for j in block) for block in intervals)
                retained = selected or not success
                ones = mask.bit_count()
                if retained:
                    total += q ** ones * (1 - q) ** (coords - ones)
            formula = q + (1 - q) * product(1 - q ** length for length in lengths)
            assert total == formula
            probabilities.append({"lengths": list(lengths), "q": str(q), "retention": str(total)})
            cases += 1
    return {"independent_probability_identities": cases, "examples": probabilities}


def product(xs):
    value = Fraction(1)
    for x in xs:
        value *= x
    return value


def bfs(adj, x):
    dist = {x: 0}
    queue = deque([x])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v not in dist:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                queue.append(v)
    return dist


def fixture_checks():
    p = 3
    vertices = list(itertools.product(range(p), repeat=3))
    identity = (0, 0, 0)
    a, b, z = (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)
    assert all(power(x, p) == identity for x in vertices)
    # Four elements of H=<b,z> and their explicit positive words.
    words = [(b,), (z,), (b, z), (b, b, z)]
    bs = []
    for word in words:
        value = identity
        for letter in word:
            value = mul(value, letter)
        bs.append(value)
    cs = [mul(a, x) for x in bs]
    sets = [{power(c, i) for i in range(1, p)} for c in cs]
    assert len(set.union(*sets)) == sum(map(len, sets))
    assert identity not in set.union(*sets)
    support = [identity] + sorted(set.union(*sets))

    # Cyclic backbone: remove one positive edge from every b- and z-cycle.
    backbone = set()
    cycle_of = {}
    for generator in (b, z):
        seen = set()
        for x in vertices:
            if x in seen:
                continue
            orbit = [mul(x, power(generator, i)) for i in range(p)]
            seen.update(orbit)
            deleted_source = min(orbit)
            for v in orbit:
                cycle_of[(generator, v)] = deleted_source
                if v != deleted_source:
                    backbone.add(edge(v, mul(v, generator)))
    assert len(backbone) == 2 * len(vertices) * (p - 1) // p

    def append_backbone_step(path, generator):
        v = path[-1]
        endpoint = mul(v, generator)
        if edge(v, endpoint) in backbone:
            path.append(endpoint)
        else:
            inverse = power(generator, p - 1)
            for _ in range(p - 1):
                path.append(mul(path[-1], inverse))
            assert path[-1] == endpoint

    max_word_length = max(map(len, words))
    proven_bound = (p - 1) * (p * max_word_length + 1)
    mask_cases = route_cases = shortest_path_cases = 0
    max_prescribed = max_shortest = 0
    witness_cases = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(support)):
        A = {support[j] for j in range(len(support)) if mask >> j & 1}
        successful = {}
        for x in vertices:
            successful[x] = [i for i, c in enumerate(cs) if all(mul(x, power(c, ell)) in A for ell in range(1, p))]
        retained_sources = {x for x in vertices if x in A or not successful[x]}
        graph = set(backbone)
        graph.update(edge(x, mul(x, a)) for x in retained_sources)
        adj = {x: set() for x in vertices}
        for x, y in graph:
            adj[x].add(y)
            adj[y].add(x)
        assert len(bfs(adj, identity)) == len(vertices)
        for x in vertices:
            xa = mul(x, a)
            if x in retained_sources:
                path = [xa, x]
            else:
                i = successful[x][0]
                c = cs[i]
                path = [xa]
                for ell in range(1, p + 1):
                    for letter in words[i]:
                        append_backbone_step(path, letter)
                    assert path[-1] == mul(x, power(c, ell))
                    if ell < p:
                        assert path[-1] in A
                        path.append(mul(path[-1], a))
                assert path[-1] == x
            assert all(edge(u, v) in graph for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]))
            assert len(path) - 1 <= proven_bound
            route_cases += 1
            max_prescribed = max(max_prescribed, len(path) - 1)
            distances = bfs(adj, x)
            for generator in (a, b, z):
                y = mul(x, generator)
                assert distances[y] <= proven_bound
                max_shortest = max(max_shortest, distances[y])
                shortest_path_cases += 1
            # The first non-backbone edge on any x--xa path witnesses the
            # deterministic support-ball argument used in the lower bound.
            R = distances[xa]
            ambient_adj = {v: {mul(v, g) for g in (a, power(a, 2), b, power(b, 2), z, power(z, 2))} for v in vertices}
            ball = {v for v, dist in bfs(ambient_adj, x).items() if dist <= R}
            assert any(u in ball and v in ball for u, v in graph - backbone)
            witness_cases += 1
        mask_cases += 1
    return {
        "fixture": "Heisenberg group over F_3; finite fixture only",
        "group_order": len(vertices),
        "detour_count": len(cs),
        "support_coordinates_varied": len(support),
        "all_other_selector_coordinates": 0,
        "selector_masks": mask_cases,
        "prescribed_routes": route_cases,
        "ambient_generator_shortest_paths": shortest_path_cases,
        "local_sparse_edge_witnesses": witness_cases,
        "proven_route_bound_in_fixture": proven_bound,
        "maximum_prescribed_length_observed": max_prescribed,
        "maximum_generator_shortest_distance_observed": max_shortest,
    }


def ball_checks():
    count = 0
    for degree in range(3, 13):
        for radius in range(0, 16):
            formula = 1 + degree * ((degree - 1) ** radius - 1) // (degree - 2)
            direct = 1 + sum(degree * (degree - 1) ** j for j in range(radius))
            assert formula == direct
            count += 1
    return {"ball_volume_identities": count}


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--output', type=Path, default=Path('local-sparsifier-checks.json'))
    args = parser.parse_args()
    result = {
        "status": "PASS",
        "scope": "Exact finite combinatorics and rational identities only; not a proof assistant or an infinite-group verification.",
        "cycle_boundary": cycle_checks(),
        "selector_density": density_checks(),
        "finite_group_routing": fixture_checks(),
        "ball_volume": ball_checks(),
        "unverified_by_this_script": [
            "Burnside algebra and nonamenability",
            "Abért--Weiss finite-pattern approximation",
            "infinite invariant construction and cost infima",
            "mathematical novelty",
            "either universal conjecture"
        ],
    }
    args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.output.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + '\n')
    print(json.dumps({key: value for key, value in result.items() if key != 'selector_density'}, indent=2))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
PY
python /mnt/data/torsion-local-work/replay_local_sparsifiers.py --output /mnt/data/fixed-price-local-sparsifier-checks.json

---
rg: 2
id: fpbs-burnside-common-upper-cost
kind: claim
title: Every infinite subgroup in a fixed large-odd-exponent Burnside family has the same upper cost

# Fixed Price / Benjamini–Schramm: Cairn research addition

Neither universal problem is solved in this bundle. It contains a written
finite-cluster-corrected cost–threshold bound, an explicit reciprocal routing
obstruction, a compactness obstruction, and honest open dependency nodes.
No mathematical novelty or Lean formalization is claimed.

Read `research/artifacts/fixed-price-percolation.md` for the complete arguments,
scope, published prerequisites, and the exact remaining gaps.

## Replay

From this directory, with Python 3.10 or newer:

```sh
python3 scripts/replay.py --output research/artifacts/replay.json
./bin/cairn check --json
./bin/cairn why fpbs-benjamini-schramm-universal --json
./bin/cairn why fpbs-fixed-price-universal --json
```

The first command checks finite combinatorics and rational identities only.
Cairn checks the dependency graph, not mathematical proof validity. The two
universal targets and the fixed-price-one percolation kernel remain OPEN.

## Integration into the supplied project

The `research/fpbs-*.md` nodes and `research/artifacts/` material are an additive
research delta. Their `scripts/replay.py` dependency must also be retained.
The original research files are not modified. This isolated package includes
a byte-identical copy of the supplied Cairn implementation and its required
math display assets, a small launcher, and the supplied Apache-2.0 license. The copied source notes under
`source_excerpts/` are evidence for the archive audit, not new proof nodes.

The whole uploaded project had pre-existing compilation errors, including
unavailable git-pinned artifacts in a ZIP snapshot. Its saved baseline check
is not a successful verification. Isolated validation of these additions is
reported separately in `research/artifacts/cairn-check.json`.

## Attribution

The qualitative no-nonuniqueness => fixed-price-one implication is Lyons's
known theorem, using Abert–Weiss. Standard cost facts are imported from
Gaboriau. See the proof note's references. Do not relabel these results as a
new solution to either universal problem.

# Local, uniformly expanding torsion sparsifiers

## Status and scope

This note gives a constructive strengthening of the earlier action-level torsion detour argument. It does not solve Fixed Price or the Benjamini–Schramm conjecture, and makes no bibliographic priority claim. Its substantive output is simultaneous control of edge intensity, deterministic replacement distances, locality, and pointwise expansion, using only edges of the original Cayley graph.

The construction uses the cyclic-centralizer algebra and torsion detours recorded by Donoso-Echenique–Silva [DS]. The new derivations here combine a half-boundary cycle-deletion lemma, exponentially many short disjoint detours, and an explicit local repair rule. The algebraic inputs and Abért–Weiss are imported theorems; the finite replay does not verify them. All group actions used for cost are on standard probability spaces and are essentially free and probability preserving.

The preceding note, `torsion-actions.md` in the package, permits arbitrarily small relative extension cost but explicitly does not bound paths in an arbitrary nearly optimal subgroup graphing. Here we use a particular cyclic backbone, not an arbitrary nearly optimal graphing. Consequently the geometric theorem below is not an assertion of short routes near the unknown minimal action cost.

## 1. Main theorem: the standard Burnside graphs

Fix an odd integer n >= 1003. Let Gamma_m = B(m,n), m >= 2, with standard generators a_1,...,a_m, and let G_m be its simple undirected standard Cayley graph. Let

    h_n = inf { |boundary_E F| / |F| :
                empty != F finite subset of Cay(B(2,n), {a_1^+-1,a_2^+-1}) }.

The imported nonamenability theorem gives h_n > 0. The subgroup generated by a_1,a_2 is canonically B(2,n): the homomorphism that kills the other free Burnside generators is a retraction. Thus h_n is independent of m.

**Theorem 1.** There is a constant C_n < infinity such that, for every m >= 2 and 0 < epsilon < 1, a Gamma_m-equivariant finite-radius factor of independent continuous vertex labels produces a random subgraph K_(m,epsilon) of G_m with the following properties almost surely.

1. K_(m,epsilon) is connected and spanning.
2. Its half expected degree is at most 2 - 2/n + epsilon.
3. Every nonempty finite vertex set F satisfies

       |boundary_K F| >= (h_n/2) |F|.

4. Every original generator edge has a K-path of length at most

       R_(m,epsilon) <= C_n [1 + log(m/epsilon)].

   The bound holds simultaneously for all edges. In particular,

       d_G(x,y) <= d_K(x,y) <= R_(m,epsilon) d_G(x,y).

5. The edge decisions are determined by independent labels in an ambient ball of radius at most C_n[1+log(m/epsilon)]. This is a deterministic coding radius, not merely an almost-sure finite random radius. Equivariance is for the specified group action and generator labels, not claimed for every unlabeled-graph automorphism.
6. The total edge intensity of retained types a_3,...,a_m is at most epsilon.

The same numerical cost, replacement-distance and orbitwise expansion bounds are achievable by a generating graphing of each given free p.m.p. action of Gamma_m, using only restrictions of its original generator transformations. The arbitrary-action assertion is not an iid-factor assertion and does not replace the given action by a Bernoulli extension.

The half-degree bound is a bound for a specific graphing, and hence an upper bound on action cost. It is not an equality for the infimum defining the action's cost.

For m=2 the construction is just the cyclic backbone of Section 2. For m>=3, Sections 3–5 produce the additional edges.

## 2. The cyclic backbone and a pointwise half-boundary lemma

**Lemma 2.1.** Let C be a finite simple cycle and delete any one edge e. For every subset A of its vertices,

    |boundary_(C-e) A| >= (1/2) |boundary_C A|.

**Proof.** The number of cycle edges crossing A is either zero or at least two. Deletion removes at most one of them. QED.

For each positive a_1-cycle and each positive a_2-cycle, delete the outgoing edge at the unique minimum-priority vertex. Use independent continuous priorities; uniqueness holds simultaneously on the countably many finite cycles almost surely. Each generator has order n, so each such cycle becomes a path of n-1 edges. Every removed edge has a replacement path of length n-1.

Call the union of the resulting paths L. Its components are precisely the left cosets of H=<a_1,a_2>. Its edge intensity is exactly

    (1/2) E deg_L(o) = 2 - 2/n.                         (2.1)

To justify the count, each directed positive generator edge has a distinct underlying undirected edge, since n is odd and at least 3. A proportion 1/n of its sources are the selected cycle minimum. Incoming and outgoing intensities agree by invariance. There is no overlap between the two generator edge types.

Apply Lemma 2.1 separately to the a_1-cycles and a_2-cycles. For every finite F,

    |boundary_L F|
       >= (1/2) |boundary_(full a_1,a_2 graph) F|
       >= (h_n/2)|F|.                                  (2.2)

The last step sums the Cayley expansion inequality over the finitely many H-cosets met by F. The first graph may be disconnected when H is proper, but every component is infinite and expanding. Additional edges preserve (2.2). This is the reason later sparsification does not destroy the expansion constant.

The backbone rule has bounded radius at most n in the original graph.

## 3. Short independent torsion detours

We state this portion more generally. Suppose a group Gamma has abelian centralizers of nonidentity elements, all of size at most n. Distinct such centralizers have trivial intersection. Indeed, if w != e lies in C(u) intersect C(v), then u,v lie in the abelian C(w) and commute. Abelianness of C(u) now implies C(u) subset C(v), and symmetry gives equality.

In a subgroup of B(m,n), the required centralizer properties follow by intersecting its centralizers with the ambient cyclic centralizers of size n. Nonidentity element orders are at most n and odd.

Let H=<s,t> be a nonamenable subgroup with s,t drawn from the chosen generating set. Write h for the edge expansion constant of its degree-four Cayley graph, and

    gamma = 1 + h/4 > 1.

Its intrinsic balls satisfy

    |B_H(L)| >= gamma^L.                                (3.1)

Indeed, at least h|B_H(L)| boundary edges lead out of B_H(L), and each new vertex accounts for at most four of them. Thus |B_H(L+1)| >= (1+h/4)|B_H(L)|, starting from |B_H(0)|=1.

Fix an extra generator a outside H. All elements of a B_H(L) are nonidentity. A centralizer contains at most n of them, so a B_H(L) meets at least |B_H(L)|/n distinct centralizers. If |B_H(L)| >= nk, choose

    c_i = a b_i,   b_i in B_H(L),   1 <= i <= k,

in distinct centralizers. Set d_i = ord(c_i), and

    P_i = {c_i, c_i^2, ..., c_i^(d_i-1)}.

The sets P_i are pairwise disjoint, exclude the identity, and d_i <= n. Every point of every P_i has ambient word length at most (n-1)(L+1).

This is the local independence resource: exponentially many choices in L, with at most n-1 required label tests per choice. The sets of tested coordinates are disjoint for one root and one extra generator. No independence between the final retained edges at different roots is asserted or needed.

## 4. The selector and paid-repair rule

For each extra generator a use its own iid vertex field U_(x,a), uniform in [0,1]. Write

    A_a = {x : U_(x,a) < q}.

A vertex x is a failure if every candidate detour has an unselected required point:

    D_a = {x : for every i, some 1 <= ell < d_i
                    has x c_i^ell not in A_a }.

Retain the positive a-edge {x,xa} precisely when x belongs to A_a union D_a. The rule pays directly for every failure.

Because the P_i are disjoint and do not contain the identity, the exact edge-retention probability is

    P(x in A_a union D_a)
       = q + (1-q) product_i (1-q^(d_i-1))
       <= q + exp(-k q^(n-1)).                           (4.1)

The first equality uses independence of the label at x from all detour labels. The final inequality uses 0<q<1 and d_i<=n.

**Deterministic routing.** If the a-edge at x was not retained, x is not a failure, and some i has x c_i^ell in A_a for every 1<=ell<d_i. Route backwards from xa to x:

    xa --b_i--> x c_i --a--> x c_i a --b_i--> x c_i^2
       --a--> ... --b_i--> x c_i^(d_i) = x.

There are d_i b_i-steps and d_i-1 a-steps. Every displayed a-step starts at a selected point, and is therefore retained. Replace each b_i-step by a word of length at most L in s^+-1,t^+-1, and each of its letters by a backbone path of length at most n-1. The total path length is at most

    d_i(n-1)L + (d_i-1) <= (n-1)(nL+1).                 (4.2)

If the a-edge was retained, its replacement path simply has length one. Therefore (4.2), not merely a high-probability estimate, holds for every a-edge in every selector configuration. Continuous priorities are needed only for unique cycle minima; labels on null tie events can be assigned arbitrary outputs.

The decision for an outgoing a-edge inspects only the source label and the labels at xP_i. The full root star also includes incoming positive edges, so a coding-radius bound is

    max{ n, (n-1)(L+1)+1 }.                              (4.3)

A single iid continuous mark can encode all finitely many independent fields used at each vertex.

## 5. Explicit parameters and the rank-uniform bound

For the standard Gamma_m with m>=3 let r=m-2, take H=<a_1,a_2>, and choose

    q = epsilon/(2r),
    k = ceiling( q^(-(n-1)) log(1/q) ),
    L = ceiling( log(nk) / log(1+h_n/4) ).                (5.1)

Then gamma^L >= nk provides k short detours for each extra generator. Equation (4.1) is at most 2q, so summing over the r extra types gives total extra intensity at most epsilon.

Equation (2.1) gives the asserted total half-degree. Equations (2.2), (4.2), and (4.3) give expansion, routes, and locality. Every original generator edge has a replacement, so the graph is connected and spanning.

For clarity about the big-O constant, q<=1/2 and

    log(nk) <= log(2n) + (n-1)log(1/q) + log log(1/q).

For t>0, log t <= t, so the right side is bounded by log(2n)+n log(1/q). Hence there is C_n, depending only on n and h_n, such that both the coding and routing radii are at most

    C_n [1 + log(m/epsilon)].                            (5.2)

The number of tests k is large, approximately q^(-(n-1))log(1/q). A logarithmic radius is not a claim of small computational running time, few inspected vertices, or practical efficiency. The constants can be very large.

This proves the iid assertion of Theorem 1.

## 6. Every generating set of every infinite finitely generated subgroup

**Theorem 2.** Let Gamma be an infinite finitely generated subgroup of B(m,n), with odd n>=1003. For any finite symmetric generating set S excluding the identity, choose representatives S_+ of its inverse pairs. There are noncommuting s,t in S_+. Put H=<s,t> and let h_H be the edge expansion constant of Cay(H,{s^+-1,t^+-1}). Then h_H>0. For every 0<epsilon<1 there is a finite-radius FIID connected spanning subgraph K_epsilon of Cay(Gamma,S) such that

    (1/2)E deg_K(o)
       <= (1-1/ord(s)) + (1-1/ord(t)) + epsilon
       <= 2-2/n+epsilon,                                (6.1)

    h(K_epsilon) >= h_H/2,                              (6.2)

and its original-edge routing and coding radii are at most

    C_(Gamma,S,n) [1+log(1/epsilon)].                    (6.3)

The retained edge intensity for positive generator types outside {s,t} is at most epsilon; types in H other than s,t may all be omitted. Every given free p.m.p. action admits the corresponding graphing version.

**Algebraic justification.** If all generators commuted, Gamma would lie in the finite cyclic centralizer of one of them, contrary to infinitude. Thus s,t exist. Their subgroup is noncyclic, and [I, DS] gives a subgroup isomorphic to B(infinity,n), hence B(2,n). Since B(2,n) is nonamenable, H is nonamenable. These are imported results, not supplied by the finite tests.

**Construction.** Delete one edge from each finite s- and t-cycle, of lengths ord(s), ord(t). The cycle lemma and the H-coset decomposition prove (6.2). Every backbone letter has a route of length at most n-1.

Let r=|S_+ outside H|. For r>0, use (5.1) with h_H in place of h_n and one independent selector field for each such generator. For the finitely many generators in (S_+ intersect H) outside {s,t}, choose fixed s,t-words. Let ell_0 be their maximum length, or zero if there are none, and omit all their original edge types. They are replaced by paths of length at most (n-1)ell_0. A bound valid for all original edges is

    R_epsilon = (n-1) max{1, ell_0, nL+1}.               (6.4)

If r=0, Gamma=H and the backbone alone suffices, with a constant radius. Otherwise Sections 3–5 prove all assertions. QED.

The construction in fact only needs bounded finite abelian centralizers, no involutions, and the existence of a nonamenable two-generator subgroup generated by two of the chosen generators. The Burnside algebra is used to ensure these hypotheses for all the specified generating sets.

## 7. Implementing the construction in each original free action

Fix a given essentially free p.m.p. action and discard an invariant null set so that every orbit is free. We use right-action notation x->xg. A Borel injective real label on the action space picks a unique minimum on each finite s- and t-orbit. Delete its outgoing generator edge. These measurable finite-class selectors have measures exactly 1/ord(s) and 1/ord(t). Thus the backbone graphing cost is exactly the first two terms of (6.1), without requiring iid priorities.

For each extra a outside H choose q=epsilon/(4r), k and L as above. By Abért–Weiss [AW], the original free action weakly contains the Bernoulli shift. Concretely, for

    F_a={e} union P_1 union ... union P_k

and eta>0 there is a measurable A_a in the original space whose binary F_a-pattern has law within eta in total variation of the iid Bernoulli(q) pattern. Finite-pattern total variation follows by approximating the finitely many atom probabilities to sufficiently small error.

Define D_a by the identical finite formula from Section 4, and retain the restriction of T_a to A_a union D_a. This union is a single finite-pattern event. Its measure is therefore at most

    q + exp(-kq^(n-1)) + eta <= 2q+eta.

Choose eta<=q. Each extra type costs at most 3q, and their total is below epsilon. No independence between different A_a, or between these sets and the backbone selector, is necessary.

All routing and boundary statements are deterministic properties of the selected graph. Thus they hold on every free orbit in the conull set, with the same bounds. Every failed detour is repaired directly, so no exceptional positive-measure failures or limiting-connectivity assertions enter the proof.

This graphing is a family of restrictions of the original finite list of generator transformations. Its cost is the sum of their domain measures, which agrees with half of the average orbit degree since inverse duplicates and involutions have been excluded.

The arbitrary-action construction does not claim to be a Bernoulli factor, to have iid output, or to have a finite coding radius relative to any preassigned labeling of that action. Its rules depend on finitely many translates of newly selected measurable sets. Its graph-metric replacement bound is deterministic and logarithmic as stated.

## 8. The logarithmic route order is necessary for sparse coset reconnection

**Proposition 3.** Let G=Cay(Gamma,S) be d-regular with d>=3, H<=Gamma, and a in S outside H. Let J be an invariant random subgraph of G. Call an edge external when its generator label lies outside H, and suppose its intensity is

    delta=(1/2)E deg_external(o)>0.

If d_J(o,a)<=R almost surely, then

    1 <= delta |B_G(o,R)|.                              (8.1)

**Proof.** A path between o and a cannot consist solely of H-generator steps. A path of length at most R stays in B_G(o,R), so there is an external retained edge with both endpoints in that ball. Hence

    1 <= E[# external retained edges internal to B_G(o,R)]
      <= (1/2) sum_(v in B_G(o,R)) E deg_external(v)
      = delta |B_G(o,R)|.

The half-sum counts internal edges exactly once and may also count outgoing edges by halves, so its use as an upper bound is valid. QED.

The standard degree bound

    |B_G(o,R)| <= 1 + d[(d-1)^R-1]/(d-2)

then implies, for delta<=1,

    R >= log(1 + ((d-2)/d)(delta^(-1)-1)) / log(d-1).     (8.2)

In particular, any family with external intensity at most epsilon and almost-sure deterministic replacement radii needs R=Omega_G(log(1/epsilon)). When H is proper, the construction in Theorem 2 has exactly this order in epsilon. For the iid parameter choice, the external intensity is also at least rq=epsilon/2, so epsilon represents the actual intensity up to a factor two.

This optimal-order assertion concerns sparse inter-coset reconnection and the limit epsilon->0 for a fixed graph. It does not assert optimal constants, optimal rank dependence, optimal average degree, or any lower bound on the cost of the action. If H=Gamma the proposition is inapplicable and constant routes may suffice.

## 9. Robustness under further independent percolation

**Lemma 4.** Any infinite connected locally finite graph X with edge expansion at least h>0 has

    p_c(X) <= 1/(1+h).                                  (9.1)

Here p_c is the infimum retention parameter giving the root an infinite cluster. Root choice is immaterial on a connected graph.

**Proof.** Explore the root cluster by testing unexamined edges with exactly one endpoint already discovered. An open test discovers one new vertex. Continue until no such unexamined edge exists, or indefinitely, using a fixed exhaustive ordering. If exploration ends in a finite cluster C, the number S of successful tests is |C|-1, and the number F of failed tests is at least |boundary_X C|. Therefore

    F-hS >= h.

The tests reveal fresh independent Bernoulli(p) variables. Pad the coin sequence by independent coins after a possible stopping time. The process Z=F-hS has increments 1 with probability 1-p and -h with probability p. If p>1/(1+h), its drift is negative. There is a positive probability it never reaches h. For completeness, choose t>0 with E exp(t increment)<1, which is possible by the negative derivative at t=0. Then exp(t Z_j) is a nonnegative supermartingale starting at one; the maximal inequality bounds the probability of ever reaching h by exp(-th)<1. On the complementary event exploration cannot stop in a finite cluster. This proves positive survival probability and (9.1). QED.

Apply this conditional on any realization in Theorem 1 or 2:

    p_c(K_(m,epsilon)) <= 1/(1+h_n/2) < 1,              (9.2)

or p_c(K_epsilon)<=1/(1+h_H/2). The first bound is uniform in rank m and epsilon; the second is uniform in epsilon for the specified backbone.

This supplies robustness to a positive density of further independent deletions, not merely the absence of individual bridges. In the earlier vertical-fiber example on a tree times Z, the backbone fibers were amenable and the retained graphs' critical thresholds tended to one. The present backbone is nonamenable and its pointwise boundary lower bound prevents that particular fragility mechanism.

The law of K itself is dependent, even though it is produced from independent labels. Conditional independent thinning of K is not ordinary uniform-parameter Bernoulli percolation on the original Cayley graph. Neither (9.2) nor the expanding construction proves p_c(G)<p_u(G).

## 10. What has been gained, and the unsolved core

The prior bound 2-2/n is not reduced here. What is added is a much stronger realization of it: original-edge graphings in every free action; a block FIID realization for Bernoulli actions; deterministic logarithmic replacement paths; rank-independent positive expansion in the standard family; robustness to subsequent independent deletion; and a matching-order lower bound for sparse coset reconnection.

The two-generator core still has graphing cost 2-2/n. Replacing that core by arbitrary nearly optimal subgroup graphings loses the explicit cycle geometry and the route/expansion proof. Reducing the core to one cyclic generator makes the subgroup finite, eliminating the infinite supply of disjoint detours used in Sections 3–5. Thus iteration of the construction as written does not force cost one.

The common maximal Burnside cost c_n in the earlier note remains undetermined. The two explicitly specified actions there are not proved to have different costs. Both universal Cairn goals remain OPEN. This note gives a constructive positive theorem, not a proof that the remaining obstruction has disappeared.

## 11. Verification, reproducibility, and package semantics

Run the standard-library replay script:

    python3 scripts/replay_local_sparsifiers.py --output research/artifacts/local-sparsifier-checks.json

It checks:

- 28,216 exact cycle-cut/deletion cases for odd cycle lengths 3,5,7,9,11;
- 18 exact rational identities for the independent selector/repair probability;
- 512 selector masks on a finite 27-element Heisenberg fixture, including 13,824 prescribed routes, 41,472 actual generator distances, and 13,824 local sparse-edge witnesses;
- 160 exact ball-volume formula identities.

The finite Heisenberg fixture is not asserted to satisfy the infinite Burnside hypotheses. Its disjoint torsion witnesses are explicitly checked. It tests the local route-and-repair mechanism, not the existence of witnesses in the infinite groups. In that fixture the maximum observed shortest generator replacement distance is 4, and the maximum constructed detour length is 15, below the proved fixture bound 20.

The script does not verify Burnside algebra, weak containment, infinite equivariance, measure-theoretic cost infima, percolation survival in infinite graphs, or priority. The written proofs and cited inputs handle those issues; none has been formalized in a proof assistant here.

Cairn checks dependency and artifact consistency. An ESTABLISHED node records an asserted written proof or cited theorem, not independent mathematical certification. Earlier package content is retained as provenance and has not all been re-audited in this continuation. Both universal target nodes are deliberately not given solved routes.

## References

Lemma 2.3 (centralizer intersections), Lemma 2.4 (cyclic centralizers), Theorem 2.5 (noncyclic-subgroup embeddings), introduction (Adian nonamenability), and Proposition 2.7 (torsion-detour mechanism). Their group-cost theorem concerns the infimum over actions, not fixed price.
https://arxiv.org/html/2608.20472v1

[I] S. V. Ivanov, *On subgroups of free Burnside groups of large odd exponent*, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 47 (2003), 299–304; arXiv:math/0210191. Every noncyclic subgroup contains B(infinity,n) for sufficiently large odd exponent; the n>=1003 range used here is recorded with the later refinement in [DS, Theorem 2.5].

[AW] Miklos Abert and Benjamin Weiss, *Bernoulli actions are weakly contained in any free action*, arXiv:1103.1063v2. Theorem 1 supplies finite-pattern approximation in the original free action. No extension of that action is substituted in Section 7.

def ball_checks():
    count = 0
    for degree in range(3, 13):
        for radius in range(0, 16):
            formula = 1 + degree * ((degree - 1) ** radius - 1) // (degree - 2)
            direct = 1 + sum(degree * (degree - 1) ** j for j in range(radius))
            assert formula == direct
            count += 1
    return {"ball_volume_identities": count}

    Cost(alpha) <= 2 - 2/p.

old='''## 10. What has been gained, and the unsolved core

The prior bound 2-2/n is not reduced here. What is added is a much stronger realization of it: original-edge graphings in every free action; a block FIID realization for Bernoulli actions; deterministic logarithmic replacement paths; rank-independent positive expansion in the standard family; robustness to subsequent independent deletion; and a matching-order lower bound for sparse coset reconnection.

The two-generator core still has graphing cost 2-2/n. Replacing that core by arbitrary nearly optimal subgroup graphings loses the explicit cycle geometry and the route/expansion proof. Reducing the core to one cyclic generator makes the subgroup finite, eliminating the infinite supply of disjoint detours used in Sections 3–5. Thus iteration of the construction as written does not force cost one.

Both universal Cairn goals remain OPEN. This note gives a constructive positive theorem, not a proof that the remaining obstruction has disappeared.

## 11. Verification, reproducibility, and package semantics'''
new='''## 10. A genuine numerical improvement using the smallest prime divisor

**Theorem 5.** Fix odd n>=1003, let p be its smallest prime divisor, and let m>=2. Every free p.m.p. action alpha of B(m,n) satisfies

    Cost(alpha) <= 2-2/p.                                (10.1)

The same bound holds for every free action of every infinite finitely generated subgroup of B(m,n).

**Proof for the whole Burnside group.** Put ell=n/p and choose

    s=a_1^ell,   t=a_2^ell.

Both elements have order exactly p. They do not commute. Indeed, the ambient centralizer C(s) is cyclic of order n and contains the order-n element a_1, so C(s)=<a_1>. If t commuted with s, it would belong to <a_1> intersect <a_2>. This intersection is trivial, as witnessed by the independent coordinates of a_1,a_2 in the abelianization (Z/nZ)^m. That contradicts ord(t)=p>1.

Consequently H=<s,t> is noncyclic and nonamenable by the subgroup input [I, DS]. Enlarge the original finite generating set by s,t and their inverses. Apply Theorem 2 and its arbitrary-action version using this pair as the backbone. Each of the two cyclic orbit relations has a spanning-path graphing of cost 1-1/p. For every epsilon>0 the other generators can be adjoined at cost at most epsilon. Thus, within the original action space,

    Cost(alpha) <= 2-2/p+epsilon.

Take the infimum over these graphings as epsilon decreases to zero to obtain (10.1). This step does not claim that the infimum is attained by a graphing.

For an infinite finitely generated subgroup Gamma, use [I, DS] to find an embedded copy of B(2,n) inside Gamma. The same two power elements of its free generators have order p and do not commute. Adjoin these two elements to any finite generating set of Gamma and apply Theorem 2 and Section 7. QED.

This improves 2-2/n to 2-2/p whenever n is composite. In particular,

    3 divides n  ==>  Cost(alpha) <= 4/3,
    5 is the smallest prime divisor of n  ==>  Cost(alpha) <= 8/5.

For example, n=1005 is in the allowed range and is divisible by 3. The former bound was 2-2/1005=2008/1005, whereas the new bound is 4/3. For prime n the numerical bound is unchanged.

**Bounded-range geometric realization.** In the standard Cayley graph of B(m,n), the two added power-edge types have ambient lengths at most ell=n/p. Thus the stronger cost bound can be realized up to epsilon by a finite-radius FIID connected graph J_(m,epsilon) with all edges of original word length at most n/p, half expected degree at most 2-2/p+epsilon, and a positive edge expansion bound independent of m and epsilon. The two-power-generator subgroup and its degree-four Cayley graph are fixed inside the canonical B(2,n), so its expansion constant depends only on n.

The local construction and its parameter calculation apply to the augmented generating set. Its number of extra generators is at most m, and each step has original length at most n/p. Therefore the original-metric coding radius and the J-replacement length for each original generator are still O_n(1+log(m/epsilon)). Its independent-thinning threshold is uniformly bounded below one by Section 9.

The improved numerical graphings are not claimed to be subgraphs of the original standard Cayley graph: they may use those power edges. Expanding a power edge into an original-edge path can increase graphing cost, so it is not legitimate to retain the 2-2/p bound after such an expansion. Theorem 1 is the original-edge version, with bound 2-2/n.

## 11. What has been gained, and the unsolved core

There are now two positive conclusions. The original-edge bound 2-2/n has a much stronger geometric realization: graphings in every free action, a block FIID realization, deterministic logarithmic replacement paths, rank-independent expansion in the standard family, robustness to subsequent independent deletion, and a matching-order lower bound for sparse coset reconnection. Allowing bounded-range power edges gives the smaller action-cost bound 2-2/p, including 4/3 when 3 divides n.

The cheaper two-generator core still has graphing cost 2-2/p, which is greater than one for odd p. Replacing it by arbitrary nearly optimal subgroup graphings loses the explicit cycle geometry and the route/expansion proof. Reducing the core to one cyclic generator makes the subgroup finite, eliminating the infinite supply of disjoint detours used in Sections 3–5. Thus iteration of the construction as written does not force cost one.

The common maximal Burnside cost c_n in the earlier note is now bounded by

    1 <= c_n <= 2-2/p,

but remains undetermined. For the explicit finite-sheet action beta in that note, its proved formula Cost(beta)=1+(c_n-1)/n now gives the improved upper bound 1+(1-2/p)/n, which is 1+1/(3n) when p=3. No strict separation between the two action costs follows. Both universal Cairn goals remain OPEN.

## 12. Verification, reproducibility, and package semantics'''

### `09-08 23:28:14` — assistant / text

**The centralizer restrictions can be removed entirely.** The resulting argument gives a theorem for all countable bounded-exponent groups—and definite fixed-price-one conclusions for substantial classes, rather than another conditional comparison of two unknown costs.

The principal conclusions are:


$$
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\text{Every countably infinite bounded-exponent group with}\\
\text{finite subgroups of arbitrarily large order has fixed price one.}
\end{gathered}}
$$


In particular, combining the argument with Held’s theorem on infinite $2$-groups gives


$$
\boxed{
\text{Every countably infinite group satisfying }
g^{\,2^r}=e\ \text{for all }g
\text{ has fixed price one.}
}
$$


The bounded-exponent hypothesis is essential to the argument. The deductions below have written proofs, but I have not established their novelty or obtained independent mathematical verification.

[Complete proof note](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-bounded-exponent-progress.md)

## 1. The main theorem: every infinite subgroup is sufficient at arbitrarily small additional cost

The previous note required nontrivial centralizers to be abelian and uniformly finite. The new argument needs neither condition. fileciteturn4file0L120-L131

Let $G$ be countably infinite, and suppose there is a fixed integer $N\ge2$ such that

$$
g^N=e\qquad(g\in G).
$$

Let $\alpha$ be any essentially free probability-preserving action on a standard probability space. For $K\le G$, denote its orbit relation by $R_K$.

### Theorem A

For every infinite subgroup $H\le G$,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)
\le
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha|_H).
}
\tag{1}
$$


More strongly, once the $H$-orbit relation is available, the additional graphing cost needed to generate the entire $G$-orbit relation has infimum zero:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{relCost}(R_G;R_H)=0.
}
\tag{2}
$$


This is a statement about the **original specified action**. No random extension or substitution of a Bernoulli action occurs.

Here

$$
\operatorname{relCost}(R;S)
=
\inf\{\operatorname{Cost}(\Psi):S\vee R_\Psi=R\}.
$$

As usual, graphing cost is the sum of the measures of the domains of its partial transformations; action cost is the infimum over generating graphings. Zero relative cost is an infimum, not a claim that an attaining zero-cost graphing exists. citeturn696429view0

### The idea

**When torsion detours overlap, their overlap supplies a commuting element that can be added cheaply.**

After adjoining such elements, stop each remaining detour at its **first return to the enlarged subgroup**. This removes shared powers already absorbed into that subgroup.

Thus collisions are not merely an obstruction to the old proof. They provide the other half of a proof by cases.

## 2. Proof of Theorem A

Write the action on the right, $x\mapsto xg$, and work on an invariant conull set where it is free.

### A finite selection lemma

For a finite set $F\subseteq G$ and $\eta>0$, there is a finite measurable partition of the action space such that, outside a set of measure less than $\eta$, all points

$$
xg,\qquad g\in F,
$$

belong to different partition atoms.

To see this, take increasingly fine finite partitions separating points. Freeness gives $xg\ne xh$ almost surely for $g\ne h$. The probability that any of the finitely many pairs remains in the same atom therefore tends to zero.

Independently select the finitely many atoms with probability $q$, and let $A$ be their union. This auxiliary randomness will be removed by averaging.

Suppose $P_1,\ldots,P_k\subseteq F$ are disjoint, and define the failure set

$$
D(A)=
\{x:\text{no }i\text{ satisfies }xP_i\subseteq A\}.
$$

For the roots whose tested points lie in distinct atoms, the selections are independent. Hence

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathrm{colors}}\mu(A)=q,
$$

and

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathrm{colors}}\mu(D(A))
\le
\prod_{i=1}^k(1-q^{|P_i|})+\eta.
$$


Consequently, some **deterministic measurable set $A$** satisfies

$$
\boxed{
\mu(A)+\mu(D(A))
\le q+\prod_{i=1}^k(1-q^{|P_i|})+\eta.
}
\tag{3}
$$


Only the sum is needed. There is no assumption of an infinite independent labeling on the original action.

### First-return detours

Fix $K\le G$ and $a\notin K$. Suppose we have elements

$$
c_i=ab_i,\qquad b_i\in K,
$$

and integers $2\le d_i\le N$ such that

$$
c_i^{d_i}\in K,
$$

while the sets

$$
P_i=\{c_i,c_i^2,\ldots,c_i^{d_i-1}\}
$$

are pairwise disjoint and lie outside $K$.

Apply (3). Add the $a$-transformation restricted to $A$, and also restricted to $D(A)$.

For a failure root $x\in D(A)$, the direct edge $x\leftrightarrow xa$ has been added.

Otherwise, choose a successful $i$. Starting at $xa$, follow

$$
xa
\xrightarrow{\,b_i\,}xc_i
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}xc_i a
\xrightarrow{\,b_i\,}xc_i^2
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}\cdots
\xrightarrow{\,b_i\,}xc_i^{d_i}
\xrightarrow{\,c_i^{-d_i}\,}x.
$$

The $b_i$-steps and the last step belong to $R_K$. Every displayed $a$-step starts at a selected point $xc_i^j\in A$.

Thus every $a$-connection is generated. The additional cost is at most

$$
\boxed{
q+(1-q^{N-1})^k+\eta.
}
\tag{4}
$$


If arbitrarily many disjoint detours exist, choose $q$ small, then finite $k$ large, then $\eta$ small. This proves

$$
\operatorname{relCost}(R_{\langle K,a\rangle};R_K)=0.
\tag{5}
$$


Notice that we only require $c_i^{d_i}\in K$, **not** $c_i^{d_i}=e$. No normality of $K$ is being assumed.

### Commuting elements can also be added cheaply

Let

$$
L=K\cap C_G(w).
$$


If $L$ is infinite, choose many distinct $\ell_i\in L$. Apply the same selection argument to the singleton coordinate sets $\{\ell_i\}$. Keep selected $w$-edges and repair failures.

Whenever $x\ell_i\in A$, the path

$$
x
\xrightarrow{\,\ell_i\,}x\ell_i
\xrightarrow{\,w\,}x\ell_iw=xw\ell_i
\xrightarrow{\,\ell_i^{-1}\,}xw
$$

recovers the missing connection.

The cost is bounded by

$$
q+(1-q)^k+\eta,
$$

which can be made arbitrarily small. Therefore

$$
|K\cap C_G(w)|=\infty
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{relCost}(R_{\langle K,w\rangle};R_K)=0.
\tag{6}
$$


We also need a finite version later. If $|L|=\ell<\infty$, take a measurable transversal for the free $L$-action. It has measure $1/\ell$. Keeping the $w$-edge only on that transversal gives the same connecting path for every root, so

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{relCost}(R_{\langle K,w\rangle};R_K)
\le\frac1{|K\cap C_G(w)|}.
}
\tag{7}
$$


### Enlarge the subgroup until all remaining detours can be separated

Fix the original infinite $H$.

Zero-relative-cost extensions are closed under countable joins: distribute an error budget as $\varepsilon 2^{-j}$ among the extensions and take the union of their graphings. They are also transitive.

Because $G$ is countable, there is therefore a **largest** subgroup $K\ge H$ satisfying

$$
\operatorname{relCost}(R_K;R_H)=0.
$$

For precision, choose one qualifying subgroup for each element belonging to any qualifying subgroup, then take their countable join.

By maximality and (6),

$$
\boxed{
w\notin K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|K\cap C_G(w)|<\infty.
}
\tag{8}
$$


Suppose $a\notin K$. For every $c\in aK$, define

$$
d(c)=\min\{j\ge1:c^j\in K\}.
$$

The exponent law gives

$$
2\le d(c)\le N.
$$

Set

$$
P(c)=\{c,c^2,\ldots,c^{d(c)-1}\}\subseteq G\setminus K.
$$


Fix $w\notin K$. If $w\in P(c)$, then $c$ commutes with $w$. Moreover,

$$
aK\cap C_G(w)
$$

is either empty or a translate of $K\cap C_G(w)$. Explicitly, if $c_0$ lies in the intersection, it equals

$$
c_0\bigl(K\cap C_G(w)\bigr).
$$

By (8), this is finite.

Thus each external element $w$ occurs in only finitely many of the sets $P(c)$.

The coset $aK$ is infinite, so we can greedily choose arbitrarily many disjoint $P(c)$: each previously chosen finite union excludes only finitely many further candidates.

Equation (5) now adds $a$ at zero relative cost, contradicting maximality. Therefore $K=G$, proving (2). Appending arbitrarily cheap additions to a nearly optimal $H$-graphing proves (1). $\square$

**There is no bounded-route assumption in this proof.** A step belonging to $R_K$ can require a long path in a chosen $K$-graphing. Only existence of a finite path is used.

## 3. Concrete fixed-price-one conclusions

Theorem A immediately gives a transfer principle:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
G\text{ has bounded exponent and contains an infinite}\\
\text{fixed-price-one subgroup}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
G\text{ has fixed price one}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{9}
$$


For an infinite locally finite group, every free action has cost one. This can be seen directly: write it as an increasing union of finite subgroups of orders $h_j\to\infty$, and connect their finite orbit trees successively. The costs telescope:

$$
\left(1-\frac1{h_1}\right)
+\sum_j\left(\frac1{h_j}-\frac1{h_{j+1}}\right)
=1.
$$

The standard lower bound for infinite orbit relations gives equality. citeturn696429view0

### All infinite bounded-exponent $2$-groups

Held’s original theorem guarantees an infinite abelian subgroup in every infinite $2$-group. I checked the theorem in the original two-page paper. citeturn860594view0

A torsion abelian group is locally finite. Consequently, for every fixed $r\ge1$,

$$
\boxed{
G\text{ countably infinite},\quad
g^{2^r}=e\ \forall g
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)=1
\text{ for every free p.m.p. }\alpha.
}
\tag{10}
$$


Held’s theorem does not require bounded exponent, but our transfer theorem does. **Equation (10) makes no assertion about $2$-groups with unbounded element orders.**

### A specified family of large even free Burnside groups

The established even-exponent Burnside results supply infinitude and infinite locally finite subgroups for

$$
B(m,n),\qquad
m\ge2,\quad n\ge2^{48},\quad 2^9\mid n.
$$

The subgroup statement follows from Ivanov–Olshanskii’s theorem as presented in Ivanov’s primary-source survey. citeturn891170view1turn860594view2

Applying (9) gives

$$
\boxed{
B(m,n)\text{ has fixed price one in that range}.
}
\tag{11}
$$


In particular,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)=1
\quad\text{for every free p.m.p. action of }B(2,2^{48}).
}
$$


The exponent range is conservative, not asserted optimal. This conclusion does not depend on determining the unknown odd-exponent constant from our earlier action-pair construction.

## 4. A quantitative theorem from large finite subgroups

The centralizer argument also yields a result that does **not** assume the existence of a nested family of finite subgroups or an infinite amenable subgroup.

Write

$$
C^*(G)=\sup_\alpha\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha).
$$


### Theorem B

If $G$ is countably infinite, $g^N=e$ for every $g$, and $G$ contains a finite subgroup of order $h\ge3$, then

$$
\boxed{
C^*(G)\le
1+
\left(\frac{(N-1)\log h}{h}\right)^{1/N}.
}
\tag{12}
$$


Therefore

$$
\boxed{
\text{unbounded finite subgroup orders}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{fixed price one}.
}
\tag{13}
$$


Here is the proof, including the point where a careless infinite-limit argument could otherwise fail.

### A finite packing-versus-centralizer dichotomy

Let $K$ be finite, $|K|=t$, and $a\notin K$. Use the first-return sets $P(c)$ for $c\in aK$.

For an integer $k\ge2$, either there are $k$ disjoint sets, or a maximal disjoint family has fewer than $k$ members. In the second case, its union $W$ has

$$
|W|\le(k-1)(N-1)
$$

and intersects every $P(c)$.

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
t
&\le\sum_{w\in W}\#\{c\in aK:w\in P(c)\}\\
&\le\sum_{w\in W}|aK\cap C_G(w)|\\
&\le\sum_{w\in W}|K\cap C_G(w)|.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus some $w\in W\subseteq G\setminus K$ satisfies

$$
|K\cap C_G(w)|
\ge\frac{t}{(k-1)(N-1)}.
$$

By (7), adjoining this $w$ costs at most

$$
\boxed{
\frac{(k-1)(N-1)}{t}.
}
\tag{14}
$$


So either we have many disjoint detours for $a$, or we have a cheap way to enlarge $K$.

### Choose parameters so both alternatives are cheap

Set

$$
q_t=\left(\frac{(N-1)\log t}{t}\right)^{1/N}.
$$

For $t\ge3$, this decreases as $t$ increases.

Assume $q_t<1$, and choose

$$
k=\left\lceil\frac{tq_t}{N-1}\right\rceil.
$$

Then

$$
kq_t^{N-1}\ge\log t,
$$

so

$$
(1-q_t^{N-1})^k\le\frac1t.
$$

Also,

$$
\frac{(k-1)(N-1)}t<q_t.
\tag{15}
$$


A free finite-$K$ action has a generating treeing of cost $1-1/t$: choose one representative in each finite orbit and join it to the other $t-1$ points.

Now the two alternatives become:

**Disjoint detours.** The relation of $\langle K,a\rangle$ can be generated at cost at most

$$
\left(1-\frac1t\right)
+\left(q_t+\frac1t+\eta\right)
=1+q_t+\eta.
\tag{16}
$$


**A centralizer enlargement.** There is $w\notin K$ whose connections can be added at cost less than $q_t$, giving a graphing for $\langle K,w\rangle$ of cost less than

$$
1-\frac1t+q_t.
\tag{17}
$$


### Enlarge finite groups, but do not accumulate their costs

Fix an arbitrary free action. If $G$ is locally finite, its cost is already one.

Otherwise, beginning with the given finite subgroup of order $h$, append generators until the first infinite step. This supplies a finite overgroup $K_0$ and an element $a$ with

$$
\langle K_0,a\rangle\text{ infinite}.
$$


Apply the dichotomy.

If disjoint detours occur, (16) bounds the action on an infinite subgroup. Theorem A extends that bound to all of $G$.

If a centralizer enlargement produces an infinite $\langle K,w\rangle$, use (17) and Theorem A instead.

If $\langle K,w\rangle$ is still finite, replace $K$ by that larger finite subgroup and repeat.

**At each finite stage, use a fresh optimal finite-group graphing.** Earlier finite-extension costs are discarded, not added to the final bill. This is legitimate because the enlarged finite group contains all the earlier groups. The same $a$ remains usable: $\langle K,a\rangle$ still contains the original infinite subgroup.

Either an infinite subgroup is reached after finitely many steps, giving cost at most

$$
1+q_{|K|}\le1+q_h,
$$

or there is an infinite increasing chain of finite subgroups. Its union is a genuine infinite locally finite subgroup, whose action has cost one. Apply Theorem A.

This proves (12) when $q_h<1$.

For completeness, the remaining case is covered by a useful auxiliary bound:

$$
\boxed{C^*(G)<2.}
\tag{18}
$$

Indeed, in the non-locally-finite case, stop at the first infinite prefix of a finite generating list. It has the form $\langle F,a\rangle$, with $F$ finite and $a$ of finite order $m$. Combining their finite graphings gives

$$
C^*(G)\le
\left(1-\frac1{|F|}\right)
+\left(1-\frac1m\right)<2,
$$

using Theorem A to extend from that infinite subgroup. Thus $q_h\ge1$ also gives (12).

Finally, let $h\to\infty$ through finite subgroup orders and use the infinite-action lower bound one. This proves (13). $\square$

The infinite branch of this proof does not assert that connectivity survives a limit of increasingly sparse graphs. It constructs an actual locally finite subgroup and then a separate generating graphing for it.

## 5. What this isolates—and what it does not settle

The quantitative theorem gives a useful obstruction to positive upper cost.

If

$$
\delta=C^*(G)-1>0,
$$

then every finite subgroup of order $h\ge3$ must satisfy

$$
\boxed{
\delta^N h\le(N-1)\log h.
}
\tag{19}
$$

Since $h/\log h\to\infty$, **finite subgroup orders must be uniformly bounded**.

Thus within bounded exponent, any remaining group with upper cost greater than one must avoid the large-finite-subgroup mechanism altogether.

This does not determine the odd-exponent Burnside constant $c_n$ from the previous note. In the large odd-exponent range, finite subgroups are cyclic of bounded order, so Theorem B cannot be invoked by sending their sizes to infinity. The recent theorem of Donoso-Echenique and Silva establishes infimal group cost one and explicitly distinguishes it from fixed price one. citeturn891170view1turn696429view1

Nor does fixed price one itself prove a Benjamini–Schramm nonuniqueness interval. No percolation estimate resolving that case has been supplied here.

### Research record

The [updated Cairn package](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-bounded-exponent-cairn.zip) adds **29 nodes** and passes its dependency check with no findings. The two universal goals remain **OPEN**. The class-specific conclusions above have written proof routes; Cairn’s status labels are bookkeeping, not independent mathematical validation.

The [finite replay](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-bounded-exponent-checks.json) passed **48,584 exact assertions**, including all labelings in **5,952 finite configurations**. It checks first-return words, centralizer fibers, packing counts, repaired connectivity, and exact selection probabilities. It does not certify the infinite proofs or the imported algebraic theorems.

**The positive result is now explicit: bounded-exponent groups with arbitrarily large finite subgroups have fixed price one, and every infinite bounded-exponent $2$-group is covered. The mechanism is that a collision between detours either disappears after a first return or provides the commuting structure needed for a cheap enlargement.**
