### `09-09 11:09:08` — assistant / text

**I obtained a stronger explicit upper bound, but not a full solution.** This time the result applies to **every free action** in the Burnside family; it does not depend on constructing the still-missing high-capacity networks.

For example, the argument gives

$$
\boxed{
1\le \operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)<1.993502
\quad\text{for every free p.m.p. action of }B(2,1003).
}
$$

The elementary two-generator construction gives only $1.998006$, rounded upward.

The improvement comes from two corrections to the cost accounting: **charge the union of selected and repaired edges only once, then remove a redundant edge from every fully retained torsion cycle.** Below is the complete deduction. I make no novelty claim, and the infinite argument has not been independently verified.

[Complete proof note](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-burnside-explicit-bound.md) · [Updated Cairn package](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-burnside-explicit-cairn.zip)

## 1. The quantitative theorem

Let

$$
\Gamma=B(2,n)=\langle a,b\rangle,
$$

where $n\ge1003$ is odd. This is a common range in which the required infinitude, cyclic-centralizer, and subgroup-embedding theorems apply. citeturn929077view0

For $q\in[0,1]$, define

$$
\boxed{
B_n(q)
=
1-\frac1n
+q
+(1-q)(1-q^{\,n-1})^n
-\frac{q^n}{n},
}
\tag{1}
$$

and put

$$
U_n=\min_{0\le q\le1}B_n(q).
$$


### Theorem

Every essentially free probability-preserving action $\alpha$ of $B(2,n)$ satisfies

$$
\boxed{
1\le\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)\le U_n<2-\frac2n.
}
\tag{2}
$$


The lower bound is the standard cost bound for infinite-class orbit relations. The upper bound is proved below. Recall that action cost is an infimum over generating graphings, not the cost of one chosen graphing. citeturn929077view1

Here are evaluations at explicitly specified rational choices of $q$:

| Exponent $n$ | Elementary upper bound, rounded upward | Improved upper bound, rounded upward |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $1003$ | $1.998005983$ | **$1.993501476$** |
| $10001$ | $1.999800020$ | **$1.999128183$** |
| $100003$ | $1.999980001$ | **$1.999890481$** |

These are **upper bounds on every action’s cost**, not computed action costs. The improved entries were evaluated with outward-rounded interval arithmetic. No assertion that a numerical optimizer found the global minimum is needed: every individual value $B_n(q)$ is already a valid upper bound.

## 2. Proof: construct the graphing in the specified action

Write the action on the right:

$$
x\longmapsto xg.
$$

Work on a conull invariant set where it is free.

### A. There are $n$ disjoint torsion detours

Set

$$
H=\langle b\rangle,\qquad
c_i=ab^i\quad(0\le i<n),
$$

and

$$
P_i=\{c_i,c_i^2,\ldots,c_i^{n-1}\}.
$$


Each $c_i$ has order exactly $n$. The exponent law gives the upper bound, and its image $(1,i)$ in the abelianization $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^2$ gives the lower bound.

I claim that the $P_i$ are pairwise disjoint.

Suppose a nonidentity element $w$ belongs to both $P_i$ and $P_j$. Then $c_i,c_j\in C_\Gamma(w)$. The centralizer is cyclic, so $c_i$ and $c_j$ commute. The cyclic-centralizer theorem is the algebraic input here. citeturn929077view0

If $i\ne j$, their quotient

$$
c_i^{-1}c_j=b^{j-i}
$$

is nonidentity and commutes with $c_i$. But

$$
C_\Gamma(b^{j-i})=\langle b\rangle:
$$

the right side has order $n$, is contained in the centralizer, and the centralizer itself has order $n$.

Thus $c_i\in\langle b\rangle$, forcing

$$
a=c_i b^{-i}\in\langle b\rangle,
$$

contrary to the independent standard-generator images in the abelianization. Therefore $i=j$.

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{P_0,\ldots,P_{n-1}\text{ are pairwise disjoint}.}
\tag{3}
$$


### B. Generate the $b$-connections at cost $1-1/n$

Choose a measurable transversal for the free action of the finite group $H$. It has measure $1/n$.

Within each $H$-orbit, join the transversal point to the other $n-1$ points. These stars give a graphing of $R_H$ with cost

$$
1-\frac1n.
\tag{4}
$$


Only the $a$-connections remain to be supplied.

### C. Select some $a$-edges and repair failures

Temporarily use independent Bernoulli-$q$ labels on the finitely many points that a root tests. Let $U$ be the selected set.

A torsion detour $i$ succeeds at $x$ when

$$
xc_i,xc_i^2,\ldots,xc_i^{n-1}\in U.
$$

Its success probability is $q^{n-1}$. By (3), these $n$ success events use disjoint coordinates.

Let $D(U)$ be the roots at which all detours fail:

$$
D(U)=
\{x:\text{for every }i,\text{ some point of }xP_i\text{ lies outside }U\}.
$$

Thus the ideal failure probability is

$$
(1-q^{n-1})^n.
\tag{5}
$$


Keep the $a$-transformation on

$$
A(U)=U\cup D(U).
$$


For $x\in D(U)$, the direct edge $x\leftrightarrow xa$ is present.

Otherwise choose a successful $i$. Starting at $xa$, follow

$$
xa
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xc_i
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}xc_i a
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xc_i^2
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}\cdots
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xc_i^n=x.
$$

All $b^i$-steps belong to $R_H$. Every displayed $a$-step starts in $U$.

Therefore

$$
R_H\vee R_{a|A(U)}=R_\Gamma.
\tag{6}
$$


### D. Charge the union, not the sum

The identity belongs to none of the $P_i$. Therefore the label at $x$ is independent of the labels determining whether every detour fails.

The probability of retaining the $a$-edge at $x$ is consequently

$$
\boxed{
q+(1-q)(1-q^{n-1})^n.
}
\tag{7}
$$


This improves the earlier estimate

$$
q+(1-q^{n-1})^n,
$$

which charged a root twice when it was both selected and marked for repair.

The factor $1-q$ is justified by a specific independence statement about the finite tested coordinates. It is not an assumption that the resulting random subsets of the probability space are independent.

### E. Prune fully retained $a$-cycles

Define

$$
E_A=
\{x:xa^j\in A(U)\text{ for every }0\le j<n\}.
$$

This is $a$-invariant.

On each $a$-orbit contained in $E_A$, delete one retained edge, choosing it measurably. The other $n-1$ edges still connect the entire orbit. Thus this deletion preserves every connection generated by $a|A(U)$, and in particular preserves (6).

The cost saved is

$$
\frac{\mu(E_A)}n.
\tag{8}
$$


If all $n$ points of an $a$-orbit were selected in $U$, that orbit is certainly contained in $A(U)$. Hence, under the ideal independent labels,

$$
\mathbb E\mu(E_A)\ge q^n.
$$

The expected cost of the pruned $a$-graphing is therefore at most

$$
\boxed{
q+(1-q)(1-q^{n-1})^n-\frac{q^n}{n}.
}
\tag{9}
$$


Notice the order: **repair first, prune second**. Pruning preserves the repaired relation; it does not assume the detours remain valid after arbitrary deletions.

### F. Realize the estimate without changing the action

The probability calculation above can be implemented inside the original action.

Fix $\eta>0$. Choose a finite measurable partition that separates the distinct points

$$
xg,\qquad
g\in\{e\}\cup P_0\cup\cdots\cup P_{n-1},
$$

outside a set of roots of measure less than $\eta$.

Such partitions exist by refining finite partitions that separate points: freeness makes distinct group coordinates distinct almost surely, and only finitely many pairs must be separated.

Independently select the partition atoms with probability $q$. Outside the collision exception, the tested labels have exactly the independent law used above. The set of tested coordinates includes the full $a$-orbit because $c_0=a$.

Thus

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathrm{colors}}
\left[
\mu(A(U))-\frac{\mu(E_A)}n
\right]
\le
q+(1-q)(1-q^{n-1})^n-\frac{q^n}{n}
+\left(1+\frac1n\right)\eta.
\tag{10}
$$


Averaging supplies a **deterministic measurable choice of $U$** attaining this upper bound on the total pruned cost.

Add that graphing to the $H$-graphing from (4). It generates the full action. Let $\eta\downarrow0$ in the cost infimum. This proves

$$
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)\le B_n(q).
$$

Since $q$ was arbitrary, it proves the upper bound in (2). $\square$

No limiting sparse graph is asserted to remain connected. A genuine generating graphing is constructed for every positive approximation error.

## 3. The improvement is strict, and its size can be proved

At $q=1$,

$$
B_n(1)=2-\frac2n,
$$

recovering the elementary construction.

Put $q=1-t$. For fixed $n\ge3$,

$$
(1-q)(1-q^{n-1})^n=O_n(t^{n+1}),
$$

while expansion of the pruning term gives

$$
\boxed{
B_n(1-t)
=
2-\frac2n-\frac{n-1}{2}t^2+O_n(t^3).
}
\tag{11}
$$

Every sufficiently small positive $t$ therefore gives a strict improvement.

There is also a convenient parameter requiring no optimization:

$$
q_n=\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/(n-1)}.
$$

Then

$$
(1-q_n^{n-1})^n
=
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^n
\le\frac1n,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)
\le
1+\left(1-\frac1n\right)q_n-\frac{q_n^n}{n}.
}
\tag{12}
$$


For the optimized bound itself, the proof note establishes

$$
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n(2-U_n)}{\log n}=1.
}
\tag{13}
$$


This is asymptotics of the **upper-bound formula**, not of the actual action cost.

For completeness, the main estimate behind it is elementary. Writing $t=1-q$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1-q)\bigl[1-(1-q^{n-1})^n\bigr]
&\le t\min\{1,nq^{n-1}\}\\
&\le t\min\{1,ne^{-(n-1)t}\}\\
&\le\frac{\log n}{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Together with (12), this bounds $2-U_n$ from both sides at the scale $(\log n)/n$.

**In particular, $U_n$ tends to two, not one.** Increasing the exponent does not complete the Fixed Price argument.

## 4. The bound extends to every infinite subgroup in the family

For odd $n\ge1003$, every infinite subgroup $H\le B(m,n)$, with finite $m\ge2$, contains a subgroup $J\cong B(2,n)$. This follows from the published embedding theorem, since an infinite subgroup of an exponent-$n$ group cannot be cyclic. citeturn929077view0

The precise transfer argument needed here can be proved without assuming the earlier broad bounded-exponent claims.

Suppose a countable group has abelian nonidentity centralizers of uniformly bounded finite size. Two such centralizers that intersect nontrivially coincide. For an infinite subgroup $J$ and $g\notin J$, the infinite coset $gJ$ therefore supplies arbitrarily many elements

$$
c_i=gb_i,\qquad b_i\in J,
$$

whose nonidentity power sets are disjoint and whose orders have a common finite upper bound $N$.

The same finite selection and repair construction gives additional cost at most

$$
q+(1-q)(1-q^{N-1})^k+\eta
$$

for adjoining $g$ to $R_J$. Choose $q$ small, then finite $k$ large, then $\eta$ small. Thus adjoining $g$ has relative-cost infimum zero.

Enumerating the remaining elements and assigning summable error budgets proves

$$
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)
\le\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha|_J).
\tag{14}
$$


The centralizer condition passes to subgroups of these Burnside groups. Apply (14) to the embedded $J\cong B(2,n)$, then use (2). Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
\sup_{\alpha}\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)\le U_n
\quad
\text{for every infinite }H\le B(m,n).
}
\tag{15}
$$


This includes infinitely generated $H$. It is an upper bound over all actions, **not** a claim that their costs are equal.

## 5. Why this still does not yield the full solution

The published Burnside theorem establishes that the **infimum** of free-action costs is one; it expressly does not establish fixed price one. Our new bound controls every action from above, but leaves a substantial gap above one. citeturn929077view0

The remaining sufficient target is still Bernoulli cost one. For a finitely generated group, Bernoulli actions have maximal free-action cost, so that target would give fixed price one for the group. citeturn143090view0

There is no valid iteration hidden in the new inequality.

The construction starts with **all** $H$-connections available, then chooses a new family of retained $a$-edges. Applying the same construction again gives the same upper bound. It does not establish an inequality of the form

$$
C_{\mathrm{new}}-1
\le r\,(C_{\mathrm{old}}-1),
\qquad r<1.
$$


To obtain such an iteration, one would have to prove that the necessary alternative connections survive the preceding thinning, with a repair bill that preserves the new savings. That is exactly what has not been shown.

Likewise, the $n$ disjoint cycles used here do not supply a network capacity diverging at a **fixed** exponent. The previous cut-repair note explicitly required a separate ambient-network construction; that requirement remains unmet. fileciteturn11file0L274-L289

### Verification record

The [finite replay](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-burnside-explicit-checks.json) exhaustively checks **4,160 labelings** in regular $S_3$ and $A_4$ actions. These are finite models of the repair-and-pruning lemma, not finite approximations of $B(2,1003)$. The checks verify repaired connectivity, union probabilities, and cycle-pruning accounting.

The run passed **12,732 exact assertions**, including **234 comparisons of the interval evaluator against exact rational formulas**. The large-exponent numbers use stated rational parameters and outward rounding.

The [audit record](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-burnside-explicit-audit.json) separates these finite checks from the infinite measurable proof and imported algebra. Cairn’s dependency check passes, but both universal goals and the network-construction target remain **OPEN**.

**The concrete advance is an explicit, strictly improved upper bound for every free action in the Burnside family. The full solution still requires a cost-decreasing construction that can be continued without losing its connecting paths; this argument does not yet provide one.**

Prefer authoring in DOCX or PPTX (then converting to PDF) for text-heavy docs or slide-like layouts; use ReportLab here for programmatic PDF generation.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

---

## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

### `09-09 14:09:53` — assistant / text

**This time there is an explicit family for which the construction reaches cost exactly one—not merely a better upper bound or an unproved completion criterion.**

A particularly simple member is

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma_{13}
=
\left\langle a,b\ \middle|\ (ab^i)^{13}=1
\text{ for every }i\ge1\right\rangle.
}
$$


The argument below proves that this group is nonamenable, contains the free subgroup $\langle a^2,b^2\rangle\cong F_2$, and satisfies

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)=1
\quad\text{for every essentially free p.m.p. action }\alpha.
}
$$


The construction also yields **continuum many nonisomorphic examples with unbounded torsion orders**. Their Cayley graphs have a nonuniqueness interval by existing percolation theorems, applied after verifying the required geometry.

The advance over our earlier work is realizing the variable-order repair criterion in actual groups. That earlier criterion had no concrete nonamenable family attached to it. fileciteturn13file0L11-L25

This is a written mathematical deduction using the classical inputs identified below. I have not established novelty or obtained independent verification. Neither universal conjecture is claimed solved.

[Complete proof](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-small-cancellation-family.md) · [Cairn package](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-small-cancellation-cairn.zip)

## 1. The family theorem

Let $p_i\ge13$ be primes, indexed by positive integers, and suppose

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}q^{p_i-1}=\infty
\qquad\text{for every }0<q<1.
}
\tag{1}
$$


Define

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma_{\mathbf p}
=
\left\langle a,b\ \middle|\ (ab^i)^{p_i}=1,\ i\ge1\right\rangle.
}
\tag{2}
$$


### Theorem

Every group in (2) satisfying (1) has fixed price one. More precisely, in **every** essentially free probability-preserving action and for **every** $\varepsilon>0$, there is a measurable set $A$ with

$$
\mu(A)<\varepsilon
$$

such that

$$
\boxed{
\{\,T_b\text{ on the entire space},\quad T_a|_A\,\}
}
\tag{3}
$$

generates the whole orbit relation.

Moreover,

$$
\operatorname{ord}(a)=\operatorname{ord}(b)=\infty,
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}(ab^i)=p_i,
\qquad
\langle a^2,b^2\rangle\cong F_2.
\tag{4}
$$


A sufficient condition for (1) is

$$
p_i=o(\log i).
\tag{5}
$$

The primes can tend to infinity while satisfying this condition.

Thus the result does **not** require bounded exponent. In fact, the groups have infinite-order elements, and suitable choices have finite-order elements of arbitrarily large order.

The proof has two parts: show that the presentation preserves the necessary algebra, then build the graphing in the specified action.

## 2. Why these presentations define the required nonamenable groups

Write

$$
u_i=ab^i,\qquad r_i=u_i^{p_i}.
$$

Then

$$
|r_i|=p_i(i+1).
$$


We use classical $C'(1/6)$ small-cancellation theory. Its relevant consequence, Greendlinger’s lemma, says that a nonempty reduced word representing the identity must have a cyclic boundary segment containing more than half of a defining relator or its inverse. The theorem applies to infinite presentations because any particular van Kampen diagram uses only finitely many relators. citeturn380978view1

### The overlap calculation

Symmetrize the relators by taking their cyclic shifts and inverses. Crucially, this is a **set of distinct words**: identical rotations of a proper power are not counted as different relators.

Consider two different indices $i\ne j$. A common positive segment of $r_i$ and $r_j$ cannot contain two occurrences of $a$. Successive occurrences are separated by exactly $i$ copies of $b$ in one word and $j$ in the other.

Thus any common segment, relative to $r_i$, has length at most

$$
2i+1.
$$


For two distinct cyclic shifts of the same periodic word $r_i$, a common segment containing $a$ would align their periods and make the shifted words identical. Therefore those distinct shifts share at most a run of $i$ copies of $b$.

The inverse cases are identical, and positive and negative relators have no letters in common. Every piece consequently satisfies

$$
\boxed{
|\text{piece}|\le2i+1
<
\frac{p_i(i+1)}6.
}
\tag{6}
$$

The final inequality follows from $p_i\ge13$. This verifies $C'(1/6)$, including the proper-power issue.

### An explicit free subgroup survives

Take a nonempty cyclically reduced word in two abstract generators $A,B$, and substitute

$$
A=a^2,\qquad B=b^2.
$$


Its runs of $a$-letters and $b$-letters have nonzero even lengths. A segment matching $r_i$ cannot pass through an internal $a$-run: every $a$ in $r_i$ is isolated between $b$-runs.

Such a matching segment has length at most $i+2$: at most one $a$ at either end, with at most $i$ copies of $b$ between them. The same holds for inverse relators. But

$$
i+2<\frac{p_i(i+1)}2.
$$

So the substituted word contains no relator half and cannot be trivial by Greendlinger’s lemma.

Therefore

$$
\boxed{\langle a^2,b^2\rangle\cong F_2.}
\tag{7}
$$

In particular, the group is nonamenable and $a,b$ have infinite order.

### The torsion orders are exact

The word $u_i=ab^i$ is nontrivial: a word with only one $a$ cannot contain more than half of one of these relators. Since

$$
u_i^{p_i}=1
$$

and $p_i$ is prime,

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{ord}(u_i)=p_i.}
\tag{8}
$$


### The power sets are disjoint

Put

$$
P_i=\{u_i,u_i^2,\ldots,u_i^{p_i-1}\}.
$$


If $p_i\ne p_j$, the prime-order cyclic subgroups have trivial intersection.

If $p_i=p_j=p$ and they intersect nontrivially, then both cyclic subgroups have order $p$ and must coincide. Hence

$$
u_i^{-1}u_j=b^{j-i}
$$

would belong to a finite group. For $i\ne j$, this contradicts the infinite order of $b$.

Thus

$$
\boxed{P_i\cap P_j=\varnothing\qquad(i\ne j).}
\tag{9}
$$


This is the essential algebraic resource: infinitely many genuinely separate torsion detours.

## 3. The full cost-one proof

Fix an arbitrary essentially free p.m.p. action of $\Gamma_{\mathbf p}$ on a standard probability space $(X,\mu)$. Discard an invariant null set so that the action is free, and write it on the right:

$$
x\longmapsto xg.
$$


A graphing’s cost is the sum of the measures of its partial-transformation domains. Action cost is the infimum over generating graphings. Every free action of an infinite group has cost at least one. citeturn380978view0

We will construct generating graphings with costs tending to one.

### Keep all $b$-connections

Keep $T_b$ on all of $X$. This costs one and supplies the orbit relation of

$$
H=\langle b\rangle.
$$

In particular, every step $x\mapsto xb^i$ is already available through a finite path.

Only the $a$-connections remain to be recovered.

### Select a sparse set of $a$-edges

Fix $q\in(0,1)$, a finite number $k$ of detours, and an approximation allowance $\eta>0$.

For the moment, imagine independent Bernoulli-$q$ labels on the finitely many orbit points tested at each root. Let $U$ be the selected set.

Detour $i$ succeeds at $x$ when

$$
xu_i,\ xu_i^2,\ldots,xu_i^{p_i-1}\in U.
$$

Its success probability is

$$
q^{p_i-1}.
$$

By (9), the $k$ detours test disjoint sets of points.

Let $D(U)$ be the roots where every detour fails, and retain $a$-edges on

$$
A(U)=U\cup D(U).
$$


Since the root $x$ itself is not one of the tested detour points, the ideal retention probability is

$$
\boxed{
q+(1-q)\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{p_i-1}).
}
\tag{10}
$$


The union is charged once: roots that are both selected and marked for repair do not incur two edges.

### Every missing connection is recovered

If $x\in D(U)$, its direct $a$-edge is retained.

Otherwise, select a successful $i$. Starting at $xa$, follow

$$
xa
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xu_i
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}xu_i a
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xu_i^2
\xrightarrow{\,a\,}\cdots
\xrightarrow{\,b^i\,}xu_i^{p_i}=x.
\tag{11}
$$


Every $b^i$-step is already generated by $T_b$. Every displayed $a$-step starts at a selected point.

Therefore

$$
\boxed{
R_{\{T_b,T_a|_{A(U)}\}}=R_{\Gamma_{\mathbf p}}.
}
\tag{12}
$$


This generation statement holds for **every** choice of $U$. Independence is needed only to estimate its cost.

### Implement the probability calculation in the original action

We cannot simply assume that an arbitrary action contains independent labels at every group coordinate. Instead, only finitely many coordinates are needed.

Set

$$
F=\{e\}\cup P_1\cup\cdots\cup P_k.
$$

Choose a finite measurable partition such that, outside a set of roots of measure less than $\eta$, the points

$$
xg,\qquad g\in F,
$$

lie in distinct atoms.

Such a partition exists: refining finite partitions separate points, freeness makes distinct group coordinates distinct almost surely, and only finitely many pairs must be separated.

Select the finitely many atoms independently with probability $q$. Outside the collision exception, the tested labels now have exactly the independent law used in (10). Hence

$$
\mathbb E_{\rm colors}\mu(A(U))
\le
q+(1-q)\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{p_i-1})+\eta.
$$

Averaging gives a **deterministic measurable** choice of $U$ attaining this bound.

Thus, inside the original action,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)
\le
1+q+(1-q)\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{p_i-1})+\eta.
}
\tag{13}
$$


### Let the repair bill tend to zero

For fixed $q>0$,

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{p_i-1})
\le
\exp\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{k}q^{p_i-1}\right)
\longrightarrow0
$$

by hypothesis (1).

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $q<\varepsilon/3$, then a sufficiently large **finite** $k$, then $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. Equation (13) gives a generating graphing of cost below $1+\varepsilon$.

Together with the infinite-action lower bound,

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{Cost}(\alpha)=1.}
\tag{14}
$$


The action was arbitrary. This proves fixed price one.

There is no assertion that a limiting sparse graph remains connected. For each positive $\varepsilon$, the construction gives a separately defined, genuinely generating graphing. Nor is a graphing attaining cost exactly one asserted.

## 4. The construction can have unbounded torsion orders

The simplest example takes $p_i=13$ for all $i$. Then

$$
\sum_iq^{p_i-1}=\sum_iq^{12}=\infty
$$

for every $q>0$.

But bounded detour order is unnecessary.

Let

$$
s_1=13<s_2=17<s_3=19<\cdots
$$

enumerate the primes at least $13$, and put

$$
M_j=2^{s_j^2}.
$$

Set $p_i=13$ for $i<M_1$, and set

$$
p_i=s_j
\qquad(M_j\le i<M_{j+1}).
$$


Then $p_i\to\infty$, while

$$
p_i\le\sqrt{\log_2 i}=o(\log i).
$$

For every fixed $q\in(0,1)$, eventually

$$
q^{p_i-1}\ge i^{-1/2}.
$$

Thus the required series diverges.

This gives a completely specified group with

$$
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\text{infinite-order elements},\\
\text{finite-order elements of unbounded orders},\\
\text{an explicit nonabelian free subgroup},\\
\text{fixed price one}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{15}
$$


The conceptual point is that **the number of alternatives can compensate for their increasing length**. We do not need one uniformly short detour. We need enough separate detours that

$$
\sum_i q^{\text{number of required new edges}}
$$

diverges at every positive selection density.

## 5. This yields continuum many groups, not just one example

Pair the primes as

$$
(s_{2j-1},s_{2j}),
\qquad
M_j=2^{s_{2j}^2}.
$$


For each binary sequence $\epsilon=(\epsilon_j)$, choose throughout block $j$

$$
p_i=s_{2j-1+\epsilon_j}
\qquad(M_j\le i<M_{j+1}),
$$

and use $13$ in the finite initial block.

Every profile still satisfies $p_i\to\infty$ and $p_i=o(\log i)$, so every resulting group has fixed price one.

Different binary sequences give different **marked groups** $(\Gamma,a,b)$, because the exact order of

$$
ab^{M_j}
$$

recovers the choice in block $j$.

A countable group has only countably many ordered generating pairs. Therefore a single unmarked isomorphism type can account for only countably many of these markings. It follows that

$$
\boxed{
\text{the construction yields }2^{\aleph_0}
\text{ pairwise nonisomorphic groups with the stated properties}.
}
\tag{16}
$$


This argument does not claim that the binary parameterization itself is injective after forgetting the generators; the countability step is what supplies the unmarked conclusion.

### The groups are genuinely infinitely presented

If the relation

$$
(ab^j)^{p_j}=1
$$

is omitted, every nonempty power of $ab^j$ has only short overlaps with the remaining relators, whose $b$-periods differ. Greendlinger’s lemma then shows that $ab^j$ has infinite order in the omitted presentation.

Thus no listed relation follows from the others.

If the group were finitely presentable, the kernel of $F(a,b)\to\Gamma_{\mathbf p}$ would be finitely normally generated. Each of those finitely many normal generators uses only finitely many defining relations, so a finite subcollection would generate the entire kernel—a contradiction.

### Arbitrarily large Cayley balls can still look exactly free

All the arguments remain valid if the presentation starts at $i\ge I$, omitting finitely many initial relations. The divergent series is unaffected.

Every remaining relator has length at least

$$
13(I+1).
$$

For a prescribed radius $R$, choose $I$ so that

$$
13(I+1)>4R+2.
$$

Greendlinger’s lemma then excludes every nontrivial relation of length at most $2R+1$. Hence the induced radius-$R$ Cayley ball is exactly the corresponding ball in the four-regular free Cayley tree.

Nevertheless, every free action of the constructed group has cost one, whereas free actions of $F_2$ have cost two. citeturn380978view0

So the phenomenon is not visible from any prescribed finite neighborhood of the identity.

## 6. Both affirmative outcomes hold for this family—but the percolation part is imported

The presentations above satisfy classical $C'(1/6)$, and the groups contain $F_2$, so they are not virtually cyclic.

Gruber–Sisto’s theorem states that a classical $C(7)$ group—and therefore a classical $C'(1/6)$ group—is either virtually cyclic or acylindrically hyperbolic. Their theorem permits the infinite presentations and proper-power relators used here. Consequently, our groups are acylindrically hyperbolic. citeturn505921view1

Choi–Seo proves that Bernoulli bond percolation on **every Cayley graph of an acylindrically hyperbolic group** has a nonuniqueness phase. Therefore, for every locally finite Cayley graph $G$ of a group constructed above,

$$
\boxed{p_c(G)<p_u(G).}
\tag{17}
$$

Between those thresholds there are infinitely many infinite clusters almost surely. citeturn505921view0

The attribution is important:


$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{Fixed price one}
&:\ \text{the explicit graphing proof above};\\
\text{Nonuniqueness on every Cayley graph}
&:\ \text{application of Gruber–Sisto and Choi–Seo}.
\end{aligned}}
$$


I am not presenting the second line as a new universal percolation proof.

## 7. What this advances toward the original problems

The previous work had a variable-order repair criterion, but no actual group family realizing it. We now have presentations where all the requirements can be checked: exact torsion orders, disjoint power sets, nonamenability, and enough detours to reduce the extra graphing cost to zero.

There is also a useful structural distinction. In these groups,

$$
\boxed{\langle b\rangle\cap a\langle b\rangle a^{-1}=\{e\},}
\tag{18}
$$

as another short Greendlinger argument shows. Yet the full orbit relation can be generated above the $\langle b\rangle$-relation at arbitrarily small additional cost. The repair is therefore not simply using an infinite intersection between that cyclic subgroup and its $a$-conjugate.

**The remaining universal gap has not disappeared.** These presentations deliberately impose abundant relations on the words $ab^i$. Arbitrary groups need not supply them. Nor are these the fixed-exponent free Burnside groups: $a$ and $b$ here have infinite order, and the relations are imposed only on specified words, not on every element.

Thus this is a completed class-level application of the repair mechanism, not a solution of universal Fixed Price or universal Benjamini–Schramm.

### Verification record

The [finite replay](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-small-cancellation-checks.json) passed **143,311 exact assertions**. It includes 51,490 comparisons of distinct symmetrized relators, tests of 9,856 cyclically reduced words in the squared generators, and exhaustive repaired-connectivity checks for 5,440 labelings of finite regular dihedral actions.

Those finite actions test the repair lemma; they are **not** approximations certifying the infinite groups. The checks also do not verify Greendlinger’s theorem, the measurable argument, infinite cost infima, or the imported percolation theorem.

The Cairn update adds **28 nodes** and passes its dependency check with no findings. Both universal goals remain **OPEN**. The [audit record](sandbox:/mnt/data/fixed-price-small-cancellation-audit.json) separates written deductions, imported results, finite tests, and unresolved targets.

**The concrete positive result is now exact: an explicitly presented, continuum-sized family of nonamenable groups for which every free action has cost one, including examples with unbounded torsion orders. The mechanism has moved from an unbuilt repair criterion to groups and generating graphings that realize it.**

# An explicit nonuniqueness interval for the torsion-detour presentations

Research continuation — September 9, 2026

## Status and scope

This note supplies a direct quantitative Bernoulli bond-percolation proof for the **standard four-regular Cayley graphs** of the groups constructed in the preceding note, and for a larger class including finite subpresentations. It does not use their cost-one property, acylindrical hyperbolicity, the Choi–Seo theorem, or a universal pivotal estimate.

The new conclusions are an explicit interval `[7/20,37/100]`, a uniform lower bound `theta(p)>1/20`, and an explicit random-walk separation estimate. These are written deductions from the classical small-cancellation input specified below, basic spectral calculations, and elementary percolation facts. No originality, independent referee approval, or formal verification is claimed.

Neither universal Fixed Price nor universal Benjamini–Schramm is solved. This proof concerns a designated generating set of a specially presented class. It does not provide the required argument for arbitrary groups or arbitrary generating sets. Previous broad cost claims are not premises.

## 1. Statement

Let J be any subset of the positive integers, finite or infinite, possibly empty. For i in J choose a prime p_i>=13. Set

    Gamma = <a,b | (a b^i)^(p_i)=1, i in J>,
    G = Cay(Gamma,{a,a^(-1),b,b^(-1)}).

The graph is simple and four-regular by the algebraic arguments below. Let theta(p) be the probability that its identity belongs to an infinite Bernoulli bond-p cluster. Let X_k be independent simple random walk on G, with no holding step.

**Theorem.** For every p in [7/20,37/100]:

1. There are infinitely many infinite clusters almost surely.
2. theta(p)>1/20.
3. For every integer k>=300,

       P_p(o and X_k lie in different infinite clusters)>1/800.

In fact, let alpha_6 be the unique positive root of

    p+2p^2+4p^3+8p^4+16p^5+32p^6=1.

Then

    p_c(G)<=alpha_6 = 0.345997218806744...,
    p_u(G)>=(sqrt(29)-sqrt(5))/(6 sqrt(2))
                         = 0.371124620474627... .       (1.1)

The decimal values are numerical evaluations; the exact polynomial and radical expressions are the mathematical bounds. A somewhat stronger upper-threshold bound follows by replacing sqrt(29/2) in the proof with

    D_*=2 sqrt(1+sqrt(3)+sqrt(455)/24),

and is approximately 0.3716399214. No optimality is claimed.

For J infinite satisfying

    sum_(i in J) q^(p_i-1)=infinity for every q in (0,1),

the prior finite-selection proof additionally gives fixed price one. That cost conclusion is logically separate from this percolation proof. The constant profile p_i=13, J={1,2,...}, is a concrete example.

## 2. Algebra: the specific small-cancellation presentation

### 2.1. Classical input and the linear-word convention

We use the standard Greendlinger–Dehn consequence of classical C'(1/6): every nonempty freely reduced word representing the identity contains a **linear subword** longer than half of a symmetrized defining relator. This is the usual Dehn-reduced-word criterion (Lyndon–Schupp, Chapter V, Theorem 4.4); Sapir [S, Theorem 3.7] presents the diagrammatic Greendlinger lemma. The linear-word consequence is important below, rather than an unsupported switch between linear and cyclic runs. It also follows from the standard two-exterior-cells version of the lemma: at most one of the disjoint exposed arcs crosses the chosen boundary basepoint. The single-cell case is immediate, after removing any boundary spur.

An infinite presentation causes no difficulty: a particular null word has a finite van Kampen diagram, using a finite subpresentation which still satisfies C'(1/6). Proper powers are allowed. Symmetrization is a SET of distinct words, not a multiset of rotations.

Put u_i=ab^i and r_i=u_i^(p_i), with |r_i|=p_i(i+1). For different i,j, a common positive segment cannot contain two a's: the distances between consecutive a's would force i=j. Relative to r_i its length is at most 2i+1. Distinct rotations of the same periodic word have no common a-containing segment, since one a would align their phases and make them the same word; their common prefix has length at most i. The inverse cases are identical. Positive and negative relators have no letters in common.

Thus every piece in r_i has length at most

    2i+1 < p_i(i+1)/6,

because p_i>=13. Hence the presentation satisfies C'(1/6). Every relator is entirely positive in {a,b}, or entirely negative after taking its inverse, and every relator has length at least 26.

### 2.2. Two explicit free subgroups

The subgroup generated by a^2,b^2 is F_2. Indeed, substitute these into a nonempty reduced word on two generators. There is no free cancellation between its surviving syllables. Every run of a's or b's has a nonzero even length. A segment matching r_i cannot pass through an internal a-run, so has length at most i+2 (or i if it contains no a). This is shorter than |r_i|/2. The same holds for inverse relators. The Dehn criterion proves nontriviality.

Also

    <a b^(-1), a^(-1)b> is F_2.                         (2.1)

To see this, substitute u=aB and v=Ab, using capitals for inverses. Between noninverse consecutive u,v syllables there is no cancellation: the only inverse letter junctions arise from adjacent inverse syllables, which were excluded. Each length-two block has one positive and one negative letter. Therefore every constant-sign run has length at most two. It cannot contain a relator half, whose length would be at least 14. Again the Dehn criterion proves freeness.

These arguments in particular imply that a and b have infinite order and that the four Cayley neighbors are distinct.

### 2.3. A third explicit subgroup

Let c=ab and d=ba. If 1 is in J, put p=p_1. Since d is conjugate to c, there is a homomorphism

    C_p * C_p -> Gamma,

sending the cyclic generators to c,d. This homomorphism is injective.

Take a nonempty free-product normal form, alternating nonzero c- and d-powers. Choose exponents in [-(p-1)/2,(p-1)/2], since p is odd. Substitution into a,b is freely reduced. For adjacent syllables, equal signs create a doubled a or doubled b, while opposite signs create a sign change; none causes free cancellation.

A constant-sign alternating segment matching r_1=(ab)^p lies within one syllable, hence has length at most p-1<|r_1|/2. For i=2, a matching segment can contain at most one full b^2 run. Two such runs would require two c-to-d positive junctions, with an intervening d-to-c junction that doubles a or changes sign. Its length is therefore at most six. For i>=3, no full b^i run exists in the substituted word; a matching segment has length at most five. These bounds are all below |r_i|/2. Negative relators have the same bounds.

Greendlinger excludes a nontrivial normal form representing the identity. Thus

    <ab,ba> is C_p*C_p if 1 is in J.                   (2.2)

If 1 is not in J, the same proof permits arbitrary nonzero integer exponents because there is no r_1 to check, and gives

    <ab,ba> is F_2 if 1 is not in J.                   (2.3)

Only the specified subgroup statements are used below. The group is not asserted to be a free product itself.

## 3. A genuinely embedded tree and supercritical survival

Let L_6 be the set of freely reduced words on a,b,A,B such that each consecutive run of positive letters {a,b}, and each consecutive run of negative letters {A,B}, has length at most six. It is prefix closed and includes the empty word.

Evaluation of L_6 in Gamma is injective. If v,w are different words, freely reducing v^(-1)w leaves a nonempty concatenation of an inverse suffix of v and a suffix of w. Each part has sign-runs at most six; only the junction can merge two runs. Every **linear** sign-run consequently has length at most twelve. Since a relator half must be a constant-sign linear subword of length at least fourteen, Greendlinger excludes v^(-1)w=1.

Thus the prefix tree on L_6 embeds as a subgraph of G, using actual Cayley edges. It need not be an induced subgraph. Extra ambient edges can only help percolation.

From a nonroot vertex with last sign-run length j<6, there are two children continuing the sign and one child changing it. At j=6 only the sign-changing child remains. At the root there are four children.

### 3.1. A finite-offspring Galton–Watson process

Start at a vertex immediately after a sign change (run length one). Stop each descendant path at its first subsequent sign change. If this occurs after j additional same-sign steps, j=0,...,5, there are 2^j possible stopped descendants at distance j+1. These descendants form an antichain.

Under bond-p percolation, let Y count stopped descendants connected to their ancestor. Its mean is

    m(p)=sum_(j=0)^5 2^j p^(j+1).                    (3.1)

The indicators within a single offspring count need not be independent. However, different stopped vertices have disjoint unexplored descendant trees. Therefore their future offspring counts are independent with the same distribution. This is an ordinary Galton–Watson process, with at most 63 offspring.

If m(p)>1 it survives with positive probability. The corresponding infinite skeleton path has all segments open and gives an infinite open path in G. Since m is strictly increasing, p_c(G)<=alpha_6.

At p_0=7/20,

    m(p_0)=2058819/2000000>1.                         (3.2)

This is an exact rational computation, not an estimated growth rate.

### 3.2. An explicit survival-probability lower bound

Let f_j(z) be the offspring probability generating function when at most j further same-sign steps are allowed before the next sign change. Then

    f_0(z)=1-p+p z,
    f_j(z)=(1-p+p z)(1-p+p f_(j-1)(z))^2,
                                          j=1,...,5. (3.3)

Put m_j=f_j'(1), B_j=f_j''(1). Differentiating gives

    m_0=p, B_0=0,
    m_j=p+2p m_(j-1),
    B_j=4p^2 m_(j-1)+2p^2 m_(j-1)^2+2p B_(j-1).      (3.4)

Let s>0 be the survival probability of this Galton–Watson process. The extinction identity f_5(1-s)=1-s and Taylor's theorem (f_5''' is nonnegative on [0,1]) give

    1-s <= 1-m_5 s+(B_5/2)s^2,
    s >= 2(m_5-1)/B_5.                              (3.5)

At p_0, the probability that a particular root edge leads to an infinite open descendant tree is at least

    z_0=p_0*2(m_5-1)/B_5
       =23527600000/1803394208413
       =0.0130462878777... .                         (3.6)

The four root branches use disjoint edges of the embedded tree. Consequently

    theta(p_0)>=1-(1-z_0)^4>1/20.                    (3.7)

The last inequality is verified by exact rational arithmetic in the replay. Monotonicity gives theta(p)>1/20 for every p>=p_0. We are not assuming independence between any ambient clusters.

## 4. A spectral bound from the three subgroups

Let lambda be the regular representation and

    P=(lambda(a)+lambda(a)^*+lambda(b)+lambda(b)^*)/4,
    A=4P.

Define Q_0,Q_-,Q_+ as the symmetric four-point averages on the generator pairs

    (a^2,b^2),
    (ab^(-1),a^(-1)b),
    (ab,ba),

respectively. Direct multiplication of the sixteen terms gives

    P^2=(I+Q_0+Q_-+Q_+)/4.                          (4.1)

Restriction of the regular representation of Gamma to a subgroup is a Hilbert-space sum of copies of that subgroup's regular representation. By Section 2,

    ||Q_0||=||Q_-||=sqrt(3)/2.                       (4.2)

For reference, the four-regular tree adjacency norm is 2sqrt(3). The upper bound follows from a weighted Schur test with a Busemann weight giving one neighbor ratio sqrt(3) and three ratios 1/sqrt(3). Radial truncations of 3^(-distance/2) give the reverse bound. Dividing by four proves (4.2).

### 4.1. Bound for C_p*C_p

When Q_+ is not the free-group average, its Cayley graph is a cactus made of p-cycles. This follows from free-product normal form: the only simple cycle blocks are cosets of the two cyclic factors and their block-incidence graph is a tree.

For a nonempty finite vertex set W, let k be the number of full p-cycles in its induced graph and c the number of components. The cactus identities give

    |E(W)|=|W|-c+k,
    (p-1)k<=|W|-c.

Thus

    |boundary_E W|=4|W|-2|E(W)|
                  >=[2-2/(p-1)]|W|.

For p>=13, the unnormalized edge-isoperimetric constant is at least 11/6.

The needed spectral-isoperimetric inequality has a short proof. For a finitely supported nonnegative f, layer-cake/coarea and Cauchy–Schwarz give

    h||f||_2^2
       <=sum_{edges{x,y}} |f(x)^2-f(y)^2|
       <=sqrt((4||f||_2^2-<Af,f>)(4||f||_2^2+<Af,f>)).

Since the adjacency kernel is nonnegative, absolute values of general f reduce the norm upper bound to nonnegative f. Therefore

    ||A/4||<=sqrt(1-(h/4)^2)<=sqrt(455)/24.            (4.3)

The free-group value in (2.3) also satisfies this upper bound. Combining (4.1)–(4.3),

    ||A||^2 <=4(1+sqrt(3)+sqrt(455)/24)
             <29/2<(381/100)^2.                      (4.4)

For the strict rational comparison, sqrt(3)<26/15 and sqrt(455)<107/5. Their substitutions make the middle expression strictly less than 29/2. Hence

    ||A||<sqrt(29/2)<381/100,
    ||P||<381/400.                                  (4.5)

No finite quotient or truncated Cayley-ball numerical eigenvalue is used to establish this infinite-operator bound.

## 5. Nonbacktracking paths control the connectivity operator

This section holds for any infinite d-regular simple graph, with adjacency operator A and an upper bound D>=2sqrt(d-1) for ||A||. Put b=d-1 and

    sigma=(D+sqrt(D^2-4b))/2.

Let N_k(x,y) count length-k walks from x to y with no immediate reversal. Then

    N_0=I, N_1=A, N_2=A^2-dI,
    N_k=A N_(k-1)-b N_(k-2),                  k>=3.   (5.1)

The count is of walks, not probabilities. Each percolation connection has a simple open path; simple paths are among the nonbacktracking walks. Therefore the union bound over SIMPLE paths, followed by enlargement of the nonnegative sum, gives

    T_p(x,y):=P_p(x connected to y)
        <=sum_(k>=0) p^k N_k(x,y).                    (5.2)

We do NOT assign probability p^k to a walk which repeats an edge.

The recurrence makes each N_k a polynomial in A. Chebyshev's recurrence, or its two-root solution, gives

    ||N_k|| <= (k+1)sigma^k+(k-1)sigma^(k-2),   k>=2.

For example, explicitly

    N_k=b^(k/2) U_k(A/(2sqrt(b)))
          -b^((k-2)/2) U_(k-2)(A/(2sqrt(b))),

and the asserted bound follows on the spectral interval [-D,D]. Thus the operator series converges absolutely when p sigma<1. Summing (5.1),

    sum_(k>=0) p^k N_k
       =(1-p^2)(I-pA+b p^2 I)^(-1).                  (5.3)

All entries of the sum are nonnegative. Entrywise domination in (5.2) consequently gives domination of the l2 norm: apply the kernel inequality to |f| for finitely supported f. We obtain

    ||T_p||_(2->2)
       <=(1-p^2)/(1-Dp+b p^2),   p<1/sigma.          (5.4)

The inverse alone does not justify (5.4) beyond this convergence range. This restriction avoids using the other positive branch of the quadratic denominator.

For our four-regular G use D=sqrt(29/2). Then

    1/sigma=(sqrt(29)-sqrt(5))/(6sqrt(2)).             (5.5)

In particular T_p is bounded for p<=37/100. A convenient uniform estimate uses the slightly weaker rational D'=381/100. The denominator at p=37/100 is exactly

    1-(381/100)(37/100)+3(37/100)^2=1/1000.

It is decreasing on [0,37/100] and positive throughout that interval, which lies below the smaller root. Therefore

    ||T_p||<=1000,       0<=p<=37/100.                (5.6)

## 6. Nonuniqueness and separation

The use of bounded connectivity operators to exclude uniqueness is standard [H]. Here is the required argument.

If Bernoulli percolation at a supercritical parameter has a unique infinite cluster, then, by Harris's inequality,

    T_p(x,y)>=P_p(x and y both in the infinite cluster)
              >=theta(p)^2>0

for every x,y. For a finite set F,

    <1_F,T_p 1_F>/||1_F||_2^2>=theta(p)^2|F|.

This contradicts boundedness of T_p as |F| tends to infinity. Hence p_u is at least (5.5).

At every p in [7/20,37/100], Section 3 gives theta(p)>1/20 and Section 5 rules out uniqueness. The number of infinite clusters is almost surely a constant by Bernoulli ergodicity. It cannot be a finite k>=2: with positive probability a finite connected ball meets two infinite clusters, and forcing the ball's finitely many edges open merges clusters, reducing k with positive probability, contrary to constancy. This finite-energy argument leaves only 0,1,infinity. Here the answer is infinity.

For the quantitative random-walk statement put

    a_k(p)=P_p(o connected to X_k).

By (4.5), (5.6), and Cauchy–Schwarz,

    a_k(p)=<T_p delta_o,P^k delta_o>
             <=1000(381/400)^k.                       (6.1)

The probability that both o and X_k belong to some infinite cluster is at least theta(p)^2 by Harris's inequality, averaged over X_k. Subtracting their probability of belonging to the same infinite cluster (which is at most a_k(p)) gives

    P_p(o and X_k belong to different infinite clusters)
       >=theta(p)^2-a_k(p)
       >1/400-1000(381/400)^k.                        (6.2)

Exact rational arithmetic verifies

    1000(381/400)^300<1/800.

The right side decreases with k. Hence (6.2)>1/800 for all k>=300, as stated. The probabilities include both independent sources of randomness: percolation and the walk. The usual statement about each fixed parameter is intended; no unproved simultaneous uncountable intersection is being taken.

## 7. Relationship to the Fixed Price progress and the remaining universal gap

If the detour abundance condition in Section 1 holds, the prior proof constructs in every free action a graphing {T_b on X, T_a restricted to A} with mu(A) arbitrarily small. Its ingredients are the exact torsion orders, pairwise disjoint power sets, finite partition selection, and direct repair of every failure. Therefore that group has fixed price one. The present proof gives a direct numerical nonuniqueness interval for the standard Cayley graph of every such group, without deriving percolation from cost.

The percolation argument is actually valid for arbitrary finite or infinite J, regardless of detour abundance. For instance J empty gives F_2 with fixed price two, and one defining relation gives a different free-product example. Thus this common percolation interval is not evidence that all the group costs coincide.

The positivity of the defining words was essential to the embedded-tree proof. In a fixed-exponent free Burnside group, the nonempty reduced word

    (a b^(-1))^n

is the identity and has sign-run length one. It lies in L_6. Evaluation of that language is therefore NOT injective there. This is an explicit failure of the proposed extension, not a gap that can be filled by reusing the same argument.

The special subgroup norm estimates are also not available in arbitrary nonamenable groups: groups of bounded exponent do not contain the free subgroups used here. Nonamenability alone says ||P||<1, but does not supply the quantitative matching of the survival and operator thresholds.

Accordingly no proof or counterexample for universal Fixed Price or universal Benjamini–Schramm is established here. The every-generating-set and every-group quantifiers are not supplied by the explicit standard-graph bound. The earlier Choi–Seo consequence for all Cayley graphs of this class is an external qualitative theorem, not a replacement for these missing universal arguments.

## 8. Audit and finite computations

The accompanying replay checks the exact rational endpoint and survival calculations; the length-two group-algebra identity; nonbacktracking recurrences by direct walk enumeration on four finite four-regular simple graphs; finite normal forms for the auxiliary free-product and free subgroup arguments; and finite run-length combinatorics. Decimal evaluations of the thresholds are recorded separately from exact assertions.

These tests do not prove Greendlinger's lemma, injectivity for all words, an infinite operator norm, survival of an infinite branching process, or either universal conjecture. The written arguments above, together with the explicitly imported classical lemma, address those steps. A successful Cairn dependency check is not formal theorem verification or independent mathematical validation.

## References

[S] Roger C. Lyndon and Paul E. Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, Chapter V, Theorem 4.4 (Greendlinger/Dehn lemma). The diagrammatic statement and small-cancellation definitions are also given in Mark Sapir, Asymptotic invariants, complexity of groups and related problems, arXiv:1012.1325v4, Definition 3.6 and Theorem 3.7.
https://arxiv.org/html/1012.1325v4

[H] Tom Hutchcroft, The L2 boundedness condition in nonamenable percolation, arXiv:1904.05804v2. Context and the standard bounded-connectivity-operator versus uniqueness implication. The nonbacktracking majorant used in this note is derived explicitly in Section 5, rather than attributed to an unlocated theorem in this paper.
https://arxiv.org/html/1904.05804v2

[G] Damien Gaboriau, What is... cost?, arXiv:1011.2294v1. Used only for the cost comparison in Section 7 and for distinguishing group/action costs from graphing costs; not used in the percolation proof.
https://arxiv.org/html/1011.2294v1

Prior note: fixed-price-small-cancellation-family.md, retained in the bundle as research/artifacts/small-cancellation-family.md. Its cost-one construction is not an input to Sections 2–6 above.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Finite audits of the explicit-window proof; not an infinite theorem prover."""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal, localcontext
from fractions import Fraction as Q
from itertools import product
import json
from pathlib import Path
import random


def reduce_word(word: str) -> str:
    out: list[str] = []
    for ch in word:
        if out and ch == out[-1].swapcase():
            out.pop()
        else:
            out.append(ch)
    return ''.join(out)


def inverse(word: str) -> str:
    return word.swapcase()[::-1]


def run_length(word: str) -> int:
    best = cur = 0
    prev = None
    for c in word:
        sign = c.islower()
        cur = cur + 1 if sign == prev else 1
        best = max(best, cur)
        prev = sign
    return best


def reduced_words(max_len: int):
    level = ['']
    for _ in range(max_len):
        nxt = []
        for w in level:
            for c in 'abAB':
                if w and c == w[-1].swapcase():
                    continue
                v = w + c
                nxt.append(v)
                yield v
        level = nxt


def substitute(word: str, a: str, b: str) -> str:
    table = {'a': a, 'b': b, 'A': inverse(a), 'B': inverse(b)}
    return ''.join(table[c] for c in word)


def poly_add(a, b):
    z = [Q(0)] * max(len(a), len(b))
    for i, c in enumerate(a): z[i] += c
    for i, c in enumerate(b): z[i] += c
    return z


def poly_mul(a, b):
    z = [Q(0)] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        for j, y in enumerate(b): z[i+j] += x*y
    return z


def matmul(a, b):
    n = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][k]*b[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def matrix_from_graph(adj):
    return [[int(j in adj[i]) for j in range(len(adj))] for i in range(len(adj))]


def direct_nonbacktracking(adj, max_len):
    n = len(adj)
    result = [[[0]*n for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(max_len+1)]
    for start in range(n):
        states = {(None, start): 1}
        result[0][start][start] = 1
        for step in range(1, max_len+1):
            nxt = defaultdict(int)
            for (prev, cur), count in states.items():
                for nb in adj[cur]:
                    if nb != prev: nxt[(cur, nb)] += count
            for (_, cur), count in nxt.items(): result[step][start][cur] += count
            states = nxt
    return result


def main(output: Path):
    counts = Counter()
    def check(test, name):
        counts[name] += 1
        if not test:
            raise AssertionError(f'failed {name}, assertion {counts[name]}')

    # Endpoint and exact offspring-law calculations.
    p = Q(7,20)
    f = [1-p,p]
    m, B = p, Q(0)
    for j in range(6):
        check(sum(f)==1, 'offspring_pgf')
        check(all(c>=0 for c in f), 'offspring_pgf')
        check(sum(k*c for k,c in enumerate(f))==m, 'offspring_pgf')
        check(sum(k*(k-1)*c for k,c in enumerate(f))==B, 'offspring_pgf')
        if j<5:
            h = poly_add([1-p], [p*c for c in f])
            f = poly_mul([1-p,p], poly_mul(h,h))
            m, B = p+2*p*m, 4*p*p*m+2*p*p*m*m+2*p*B
    check(m==Q(2058819,2000000), 'rational_endpoint')
    check(m>1, 'rational_endpoint')
    check(len(f)==64, 'offspring_pgf')
    z = p*2*(m-1)/B
    root_lower = 1-(1-z)**4
    check(z==Q(23527600000,1803394208413), 'rational_endpoint')
    check(root_lower>Q(1,20), 'rational_endpoint')
    check(Q(26,15)**2>3, 'radical_upper_bounds')
    check(Q(107,5)**2>455, 'radical_upper_bounds')
    check(4*(1+Q(26,15)+Q(107,5)/24)==Q(29,2), 'radical_upper_bounds')
    check(Q(29,2)<Q(381,100)**2, 'radical_upper_bounds')
    up = Q(37,100)
    den = 1-Q(381,100)*up+3*up*up
    check(den==Q(1,1000), 'rational_endpoint')
    check(3*up*up<1, 'rational_endpoint')
    check(Q(1000)*Q(381,400)**300<Q(1,800), 'rational_endpoint')
    lo, hi = Q(0), Q(1)
    def mean(t): return sum(Q(2)**j*t**(j+1) for j in range(6))
    for _ in range(96):
        mid = (lo+hi)/2
        if mean(mid)<1: lo=mid
        else: hi=mid
    check(mean(lo)<1<=mean(hi), 'critical_root_bracket')
    check(hi< p, 'critical_root_bracket')

    # The sixteen-term identity is a formal identity in the free group ring.
    lhs = defaultdict(Q)
    for u,v in product('abAB',repeat=2): lhs[reduce_word(u+v)] += Q(1,16)
    rhs = defaultdict(Q)
    rhs[''] += Q(1,4)
    for pair in [('aa','bb'),('aB','Ab'),('ab','ba')]:
        for w in [pair[0], inverse(pair[0]), pair[1], inverse(pair[1])]:
            rhs[reduce_word(w)] += Q(1,16)
    check(dict(lhs)==dict(rhs), 'formal_spectral_identity')

    # Finite word tests do NOT decide injectivity in the infinite presented group.
    patterns = set()
    for i in range(1,7):
        base = 'a'+'b'*i
        length = (13*len(base))//2+1
        for shift in range(len(base)):
            pat = (base*20)[shift:shift+length]
            patterns.add(pat)
            patterns.add(inverse(pat))
    words_sq = words_cross = 0
    for w in reduced_words(8):
        x = substitute(w,'aa','bb')
        check(reduce_word(x)==x, 'square_subgroup_words')
        check(not any(pat in x for pat in patterns), 'square_subgroup_words')
        words_sq += 1
        x = substitute(w,'aB','Ab')
        check(reduce_word(x)==x, 'cross_subgroup_words')
        check(run_length(x)<=2, 'cross_subgroup_words')
        words_cross += 1
    free_product_words = 0
    exponents = tuple(range(-6,0))+tuple(range(1,7))
    for syllables in range(1,5):
        for first in range(2):
            for exps in product(exponents,repeat=syllables):
                parts=[]
                for j,k in enumerate(exps):
                    base=('ab','ba')[(first+j)%2]
                    parts.append((base if k>0 else inverse(base))*abs(k))
                x=''.join(parts)
                check(reduce_word(x)==x, 'cyclic_free_product_words')
                check(not any(pat in x for pat in patterns), 'cyclic_free_product_words')
                free_product_words += 1

    # Reproducible stress tests of the linear junction bound (sampled, not exhaustive).
    rng=random.Random(20260909)
    def allowed_word(n):
        out=''
        for _ in range(n):
            possible=[c for c in 'abAB' if (not out or c!=out[-1].swapcase()) and run_length(out+c)<=6]
            out += rng.choice(possible)
        return out
    for _ in range(5000):
        v=allowed_word(rng.randrange(1,101));w=allowed_word(rng.randrange(1,101))
        check(run_length(reduce_word(inverse(v)+w))<=12, 'sampled_linear_junctions')

    # Direct walk counts versus the adjacency-polynomial recurrence.
    graphs={}
    graphs['K5']=[set(range(5))-{i} for i in range(5)]
    graphs['octahedral']=[{j for j in range(6) if j//2!=i//2} for i in range(6)]
    for side in (3,4):
        adj=[]
        for x in range(side):
            for y in range(side):
                adj.append({((x+dx)%side)*side+(y+dy)%side for dx,dy in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]})
        graphs[f'torus_{side}x{side}']=adj
    nb_summary={}
    for name,adj in graphs.items():
        n=len(adj);check(all(len(s)==4 for s in adj),'finite_graph_degree')
        ns=direct_nonbacktracking(adj,12);A=matrix_from_graph(adj)
        eye=[[int(i==j) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
        check(ns[0]==eye and ns[1]==A,'nonbacktracking_matrices')
        aa=matmul(A,A)
        check(ns[2]==[[aa[i][j]-4*eye[i][j] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)],'nonbacktracking_matrices')
        for k in range(3,13):
            prodA=matmul(A,ns[k-1])
            check(ns[k]==[[prodA[i][j]-3*ns[k-2][i][j] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)],'nonbacktracking_matrices')
        nb_summary[name]={'vertices':n,'lengths_checked':'0 through 12'}

    # Finite cactus subsets test the edge-boundary ledger, not an infinite spectral norm.
    def cactus(order,cycles):
        edges=set();deg=Counter();n=1
        for _ in range(cycles):
            available=[v for v in range(n) if deg[v]<=2]
            root=rng.choice(available)
            cycle=[root]+list(range(n,n+order-1));n+=order-1
            for j in range(order):
                u,v=cycle[j],cycle[(j+1)%order]
                edges.add(tuple(sorted((u,v))));deg[u]+=1;deg[v]+=1
        return n,edges
    cactus_subsets=0
    for order in (3,5,7,13,17):
        for cycles in (1,2,3,4):
            n,edges=cactus(order,cycles)
            for _ in range(100):
                subset={v for v in range(n) if rng.randrange(2)}
                if not subset: continue
                inside=sum(u in subset and v in subset for u,v in edges)
                boundary=4*len(subset)-2*inside
                check(Q(boundary)>=Q(2*(order-2),order-1)*len(subset),'sampled_cactus_boundaries')
                cactus_subsets+=1

    with localcontext() as ctx:
        ctx.prec=70
        sqrt3=Decimal(3).sqrt();sqrt455=Decimal(455).sqrt()
        Dstar=2*(1+sqrt3+sqrt455/24).sqrt()
        threshold=(Dstar-(Dstar*Dstar-12).sqrt())/6
        safe=(Decimal(29).sqrt()-Decimal(5).sqrt())/(6*Decimal(2).sqrt())
        numeric={
          'alpha6_lower':str(Decimal(lo.numerator)/Decimal(lo.denominator)),
          'alpha6_upper':str(Decimal(hi.numerator)/Decimal(hi.denominator)),
          'D_star':str(Dstar),
          'p_u_lower_sharp_spectral_expression':str(threshold),
          'p_u_lower_safe_radical':str(safe),
          'theta_lower_at_7_over_20':str(Decimal(root_lower.numerator)/Decimal(root_lower.denominator)),
        }
    result={
      'status':'PASS',
      'date':'2026-09-09',
      'scope':'finite combinatorial and rational checks only; not formal or infinite-theorem verification',
      'exact_assertions_total':sum(counts.values()),
      'assertion_counts':dict(counts),
      'rational_endpoints':{'lower':'7/20','upper':'37/100','offspring_mean':str(m),'one_root_branch_survival_lower':str(z),'root_survival_lower':str(root_lower),'operator_denominator_at_upper':str(den)},
      'exhaustive_word_models':{'square_subgroup_words':words_sq,'cross_subgroup_words':words_cross,'Cp_star_Cp_centered_normal_forms_p13_max4syllables':free_product_words},
      'sampled_checks':{'seed':20260909,'linear_junction_pairs':5000,'cactus_subsets':cactus_subsets},
      'nonbacktracking_graphs':nb_summary,
      'numerical_evaluations_not_exact_certificates':numeric,
      'universal_fixed_price':'OPEN',
      'universal_benjamini_schramm':'OPEN',
    }
    output.parent.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    output.write_text(json.dumps(result,indent=2)+'\n')
    print(json.dumps(result,indent=2))

if __name__=='__main__':
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--output',type=Path,default=Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]/'research/artifacts/explicit-window-checks.json')
    main(parser.parse_args().output)

# An explicit nonuniqueness interval for the torsion-detour presentations

Research continuation — September 9, 2026

## Status and scope

This note supplies a direct quantitative Bernoulli bond-percolation proof for the **standard four-regular Cayley graphs** of the groups constructed in the preceding note, and for a larger class including finite subpresentations. It does not use their cost-one property, acylindrical hyperbolicity, the Choi–Seo theorem, or a universal pivotal estimate.

The new conclusions are an explicit interval `[7/20,37/100]`, a uniform lower bound `theta(p)>1/20`, and an explicit random-walk separation estimate. These are written deductions from the classical small-cancellation input specified below, basic spectral calculations, and elementary percolation facts. No originality, independent referee approval, or formal verification is claimed.

Neither universal Fixed Price nor universal Benjamini–Schramm is solved. This proof concerns a designated generating set of a specially presented class. It does not provide the required argument for arbitrary groups or arbitrary generating sets. Previous broad cost claims are not premises.

## 1. Statement

Let J be any subset of the positive integers, finite or infinite, possibly empty. For i in J choose a prime p_i>=13. Set

    Gamma = <a,b | (a b^i)^(p_i)=1, i in J>,
    G = Cay(Gamma,{a,a^(-1),b,b^(-1)}).

The graph is simple and four-regular by the algebraic arguments below. Let theta(p) be the probability that its identity belongs to an infinite Bernoulli bond-p cluster. Let X_k be independent simple random walk on G, with no holding step.

**Theorem.** For every p in [7/20,37/100]:

1. There are infinitely many infinite clusters almost surely.
2. theta(p)>1/20.
3. For every integer k>=300,

       P_p(o and X_k lie in different infinite clusters)>1/800.

In fact, let alpha_6 be the unique positive root of

    p+2p^2+4p^3+8p^4+16p^5+32p^6=1.

Then

    p_c(G)<=alpha_6 = 0.345997218806744...,
    p_u(G)>=(sqrt(29)-sqrt(5))/(6 sqrt(2))
                         = 0.371124620474627... .       (1.1)

The decimal values are numerical evaluations; the exact polynomial and radical expressions are the mathematical bounds. A somewhat stronger upper-threshold bound follows by replacing sqrt(29/2) in the proof with

    D_*=2 sqrt(1+sqrt(3)+sqrt(455)/24),

and is approximately 0.3716399214. No optimality is claimed.

For J infinite satisfying

    sum_(i in J) q^(p_i-1)=infinity for every q in (0,1),

the prior finite-selection proof additionally gives fixed price one. That cost conclusion is logically separate from this percolation proof. The constant profile p_i=13, J={1,2,...}, is a concrete example.

## 2. Algebra: the specific small-cancellation presentation

### 2.1. Classical input and the linear-word convention

We use the standard Greendlinger–Dehn consequence of classical C'(1/6): every nonempty freely reduced word representing the identity contains a **linear subword** longer than half of a symmetrized defining relator. This is the usual Dehn-reduced-word criterion (Lyndon–Schupp, Chapter V, Theorem 4.4); Sapir [S, Theorem 3.7] presents the diagrammatic Greendlinger lemma. The linear-word consequence is important below, rather than an unsupported switch between linear and cyclic runs. It also follows from the standard two-exterior-cells version of the lemma: at most one of the disjoint exposed arcs crosses the chosen boundary basepoint. The single-cell case is immediate, after removing any boundary spur.

An infinite presentation causes no difficulty: a particular null word has a finite van Kampen diagram, using a finite subpresentation which still satisfies C'(1/6). Proper powers are allowed. Symmetrization is a SET of distinct words, not a multiset of rotations.

Put u_i=ab^i and r_i=u_i^(p_i), with |r_i|=p_i(i+1). For different i,j, a common positive segment cannot contain two a's: the distances between consecutive a's would force i=j. Relative to r_i its length is at most 2i+1. Distinct rotations of the same periodic word have no common a-containing segment, since one a would align their phases and make them the same word; their common prefix has length at most i. The inverse cases are identical. Positive and negative relators have no letters in common.

Thus every piece in r_i has length at most

    2i+1 < p_i(i+1)/6,

because p_i>=13. Hence the presentation satisfies C'(1/6). Every relator is entirely positive in {a,b}, or entirely negative after taking its inverse, and every relator has length at least 26.

### 2.2. Two explicit free subgroups

The subgroup generated by a^2,b^2 is F_2. Indeed, substitute these into a nonempty reduced word on two generators. There is no free cancellation between its surviving syllables. Every run of a's or b's has a nonzero even length. A segment matching r_i cannot pass through an internal a-run, so has length at most i+2 (or i if it contains no a). This is shorter than |r_i|/2. The same holds for inverse relators. The Dehn criterion proves nontriviality.

Also

    <a b^(-1), a^(-1)b> is F_2.                         (2.1)

To see this, substitute u=aB and v=Ab, using capitals for inverses. Between noninverse consecutive u,v syllables there is no cancellation: the only inverse letter junctions arise from adjacent inverse syllables, which were excluded. Each length-two block has one positive and one negative letter. Therefore every constant-sign run has length at most two. It cannot contain a relator half, whose length would be at least 14. Again the Dehn criterion proves freeness.

These arguments in particular imply that a and b have infinite order and that the four Cayley neighbors are distinct.

### 2.3. A third explicit subgroup

Let c=ab and d=ba. If 1 is in J, put p=p_1. Since d is conjugate to c, there is a homomorphism

    C_p * C_p -> Gamma,

sending the cyclic generators to c,d. This homomorphism is injective.

Take a nonempty free-product normal form, alternating nonzero c- and d-powers. Choose exponents in [-(p-1)/2,(p-1)/2], since p is odd. Substitution into a,b is freely reduced. For adjacent syllables, equal signs create a doubled a or doubled b, while opposite signs create a sign change; none causes free cancellation.

A constant-sign alternating segment matching r_1=(ab)^p lies within one syllable, hence has length at most p-1<|r_1|/2. For i=2, a matching segment can contain at most one full b^2 run. Two such runs would require two c-to-d positive junctions, with an intervening d-to-c junction that doubles a or changes sign. Its length is therefore at most six. For i>=3, no full b^i run exists in the substituted word; a matching segment has length at most five. These bounds are all below |r_i|/2. Negative relators have the same bounds.

Greendlinger excludes a nontrivial normal form representing the identity. Thus

    <ab,ba> is C_p*C_p if 1 is in J.                   (2.2)

If 1 is not in J, the same proof permits arbitrary nonzero integer exponents because there is no r_1 to check, and gives

    <ab,ba> is F_2 if 1 is not in J.                   (2.3)

Only the specified subgroup statements are used below. The group is not asserted to be a free product itself.

## 3. A genuinely embedded tree and supercritical survival

Let L_6 be the set of freely reduced words on a,b,A,B such that each consecutive run of positive letters {a,b}, and each consecutive run of negative letters {A,B}, has length at most six. It is prefix closed and includes the empty word.

Evaluation of L_6 in Gamma is injective. If v,w are different words, freely reducing v^(-1)w leaves a nonempty concatenation of an inverse suffix of v and a suffix of w. Each part has sign-runs at most six; only the junction can merge two runs. Every **linear** sign-run consequently has length at most twelve. Since a relator half must be a constant-sign linear subword of length at least fourteen, Greendlinger excludes v^(-1)w=1.

Thus the prefix tree on L_6 embeds as a subgraph of G, using actual Cayley edges. It need not be an induced subgraph. Extra ambient edges can only help percolation.

From a nonroot vertex with last sign-run length j<6, there are two children continuing the sign and one child changing it. At j=6 only the sign-changing child remains. At the root there are four children.

### 3.1. A finite-offspring Galton–Watson process

Start at a vertex immediately after a sign change (run length one). Stop each descendant path at its first subsequent sign change. If this occurs after j additional same-sign steps, j=0,...,5, there are 2^j possible stopped descendants at distance j+1. These descendants form an antichain.

Under bond-p percolation, let Y count stopped descendants connected to their ancestor. Its mean is

    m(p)=sum_(j=0)^5 2^j p^(j+1).                    (3.1)

The indicators within a single offspring count need not be independent. However, different stopped vertices have disjoint unexplored descendant trees. Therefore their future offspring counts are independent with the same distribution. This is an ordinary Galton–Watson process, with at most 63 offspring.

If m(p)>1 it survives with positive probability. The corresponding infinite skeleton path has all segments open and gives an infinite open path in G. Since m is strictly increasing, p_c(G)<=alpha_6.

At p_0=7/20,

    m(p_0)=2058819/2000000>1.                         (3.2)

This is an exact rational computation, not an estimated growth rate.

### 3.2. An explicit survival-probability lower bound

Let f_j(z) be the offspring probability generating function when at most j further same-sign steps are allowed before the next sign change. Then

    f_0(z)=1-p+p z,
    f_j(z)=(1-p+p z)(1-p+p f_(j-1)(z))^2,
                                          j=1,...,5. (3.3)

Put m_j=f_j'(1), B_j=f_j''(1). Differentiating gives

    m_0=p, B_0=0,
    m_j=p+2p m_(j-1),
    B_j=4p^2 m_(j-1)+2p^2 m_(j-1)^2+2p B_(j-1).      (3.4)

Let s>0 be the survival probability of this Galton–Watson process. The extinction identity f_5(1-s)=1-s and Taylor's theorem (f_5''' is nonnegative on [0,1]) give

    1-s <= 1-m_5 s+(B_5/2)s^2,
    s >= 2(m_5-1)/B_5.                              (3.5)

At p_0, the probability that a particular root edge leads to an infinite open descendant tree is at least

    z_0=p_0*2(m_5-1)/B_5
       =23527600000/1803394208413
       =0.0130462878777... .                         (3.6)

The four root branches use disjoint edges of the embedded tree. Consequently

    theta(p_0)>=1-(1-z_0)^4>1/20.                    (3.7)

The last inequality is verified by exact rational arithmetic in the replay. Monotonicity gives theta(p)>1/20 for every p>=p_0. We are not assuming independence between any ambient clusters.

## 4. A spectral bound from the three subgroups

Let lambda be the regular representation and

    P=(lambda(a)+lambda(a)^*+lambda(b)+lambda(b)^*)/4,
    A=4P.

Define Q_0,Q_-,Q_+ as the symmetric four-point averages on the generator pairs

    (a^2,b^2),
    (ab^(-1),a^(-1)b),
    (ab,ba),

respectively. Direct multiplication of the sixteen terms gives

    P^2=(I+Q_0+Q_-+Q_+)/4.                          (4.1)

Restriction of the regular representation of Gamma to a subgroup is a Hilbert-space sum of copies of that subgroup's regular representation. By Section 2,

    ||Q_0||=||Q_-||=sqrt(3)/2.                       (4.2)

For reference, the four-regular tree adjacency norm is 2sqrt(3). The upper bound follows from a weighted Schur test with a Busemann weight giving one neighbor ratio sqrt(3) and three ratios 1/sqrt(3). Radial truncations of 3^(-distance/2) give the reverse bound. Dividing by four proves (4.2).

### 4.1. Bound for C_p*C_p

When Q_+ is not the free-group average, its Cayley graph is a cactus made of p-cycles. This follows from free-product normal form: the only simple cycle blocks are cosets of the two cyclic factors and their block-incidence graph is a tree.

For a nonempty finite vertex set W, let k be the number of full p-cycles in its induced graph and c the number of components. The cactus identities give

    |E(W)|=|W|-c+k,
    (p-1)k<=|W|-c.

Thus

    |boundary_E W|=4|W|-2|E(W)|
                  >=[2-2/(p-1)]|W|.

For p>=13, the unnormalized edge-isoperimetric constant is at least 11/6.

The needed spectral-isoperimetric inequality has a short proof. For a finitely supported nonnegative f, layer-cake/coarea and Cauchy–Schwarz give

    h||f||_2^2
       <=sum_{edges{x,y}} |f(x)^2-f(y)^2|
       <=sqrt((4||f||_2^2-<Af,f>)(4||f||_2^2+<Af,f>)).

Since the adjacency kernel is nonnegative, absolute values of general f reduce the norm upper bound to nonnegative f. Therefore

    ||A/4||<=sqrt(1-(h/4)^2)<=sqrt(455)/24.            (4.3)

The free-group value in (2.3) also satisfies this upper bound. Combining (4.1)–(4.3),

    ||A||^2 <=4(1+sqrt(3)+sqrt(455)/24)
             <29/2<(381/100)^2.                      (4.4)

For the strict rational comparison, sqrt(3)<26/15 and sqrt(455)<107/5. Their substitutions make the middle expression strictly less than 29/2. Hence

    ||A||<sqrt(29/2)<381/100,
    ||P||<381/400.                                  (4.5)

No finite quotient or truncated Cayley-ball numerical eigenvalue is used to establish this infinite-operator bound.

## 5. Nonbacktracking paths control the connectivity operator

This section holds for any infinite d-regular simple graph, with adjacency operator A and an upper bound D>=2sqrt(d-1) for ||A||. Put b=d-1 and

    sigma=(D+sqrt(D^2-4b))/2.

Let N_k(x,y) count length-k walks from x to y with no immediate reversal. Then

    N_0=I, N_1=A, N_2=A^2-dI,
    N_k=A N_(k-1)-b N_(k-2),                  k>=3.   (5.1)

The count is of walks, not probabilities. Each percolation connection has a simple open path; simple paths are among the nonbacktracking walks. Therefore the union bound over SIMPLE paths, followed by enlargement of the nonnegative sum, gives

    T_p(x,y):=P_p(x connected to y)
        <=sum_(k>=0) p^k N_k(x,y).                    (5.2)

We do NOT assign probability p^k to a walk which repeats an edge.

The recurrence makes each N_k a polynomial in A. Chebyshev's recurrence, or its two-root solution, gives
